# Body Spray SDK: AXE and Surface

> AXE (`axe/0.1`) is an HTTP protocol and a TypeScript SDK that let a website publish an agent-specific interface next to its human one: a manifest of typed actions, one result envelope with an escalation ladder (`needs_input`, `needs_human`), and a derived MCP server. Surface is the inside-out half: a running application registers its own live controls, with a reason for every unavailable one and one revision for the whole application, and `@axe/surface/axe` serves that registry as ordinary AXE actions. This file is for an agent about to integrate the SDK into an existing application. Every name below exists in this repository; each link points at the source of the claim.

AXE is outside-in. A site declares actions with `createAXE` and `action()`, wrapping functions it already has; agents discover `/.well-known/axe.json`, call `POST /axe/actions/{name}`, continue at `/axe/continue`, resume at `/axe/resume`, and read what can be done right now at `/axe/state`. Surface is inside-out. The application registers each control that matters (an `action`, a `field`, or a `collection`) with a stable `id`, a `name` that states the outcome, its `state` with a `reason`, its `effect`, and the very handler the control runs; `observe()` is an indexed snapshot at a revision and `act()` runs one control under a revision guard. Surface has three rules ([spec/SURFACE.md](spec/SURFACE.md) section 2): Surface reports, it never decides ([S-RULE-1]); same door, an act runs the control's own handler ([S-RULE-2]); one revision, every observation carries it and every act presents it ([S-RULE-3]). The seam is `surfaceActions(surface, { namespace })`: an `ActionProvider` for `axe.addProvider` whose set is `<ns>.observe`, `<ns>.ledger`, and one action per entry, with the entry's live `state` as the action's `availability` and its refusals mapped onto the ladder. Discovery, MCP, kinds, conformance, and the audit then apply unchanged.

## Decide your shape

Pick by where the truth of "can this be done right now" lives. Most applications combine one of the first three with the fourth.

- React components own the controls: call `useSurface(entry, deps)` or `useSurfaceProps(entry, deps)` from `@axe/surface/react` once per control, inside the component that already computes the control's disabled state. `deps` names every value the entry was computed from, including transient flags (saving, loading, a modal open); left out, the surface keeps reporting a control available while the UI has frozen it ([S-REV-5]). Rows rendered from a `.map` get a component that renders nothing and holds the hooks, so a row that leaves the page leaves the table. Spread `useSurfaceProps` onto the element that receives the interaction so the accessible name is the entry name ([S-DOM-1]). Refresh replaces the entry in place; only unmount unregisters, so an agent's index never jumps because a sibling re-rendered.
- Legacy or non-React DOM (HTML from string builders, jQuery, Web Components): write a pure re-scan adapter. After each render, read the application's own facts (data attributes, `disabled`, `readOnly`, lock records: the same state the renderer used to disable the control) into plain descriptors, then hand them to a module with no DOM access that calls `register` per control, `reconcile(prefix, keep)` per id prefix so rows that left the render leave the table, `setRev(appRevision)` or `bump()`, and `setObjects(() => domainObjects)`. Reasons come from one function that maps a descriptor to the application's words or null. The field setter and the action handler run the exact commit the change event or the button runs. Because the module takes descriptors and callbacks, it is testable without a browser.
- Server-side operations with no UI control: write `action()`s by hand ([docs/designing-actions.md](docs/designing-actions.md)), or derive them with `@axe/generate` from an OpenAPI 3.x document (`fromOpenAPI`), a table of zod-typed functions (`fromFunctions`), or a tRPC router (`fromTRPCRouter`), then `generate` and `registerGenerated`. The generator leaves out any operation without a description or a risk for a mutation and says so in a warning; it never invents them.
- Serving a surface as AXE actions: `createAXE({ ..., revision: surface.currentRev })`, then `axe.addProvider(surfaceActions(surface, { namespace }))`, then mount with `axeExpress`, `axeNext` or `axeNextPages`, `axeFetch`, or `axe.fetchHandler()`. The surface's revision becomes the site's: every envelope carries `rev`, a stale `expectedRev` is `conflict` before any handler runs, and `/axe/state` answers per control. For a page with no server of its own, `expose(window)` publishes `observe`, `act`, `ledger`, and `rev` at `window.__surface` for agents that drive the browser ([S-DOM-2]).
- Where the surface comes from: `createSurface({ app })` for an instance, or the module-level `surface` and its bound functions (`configure`, `register`, `unregister`, `reconcile`, `freeze`, `seedRev`, `setRev`, `currentRev`, `bump`, `onChange`, `setObjects`, `observe`, `act`, `ledger`, `expose`) exported from `@axe/surface`. `useSurface` and `useSurfaceProps` take an optional third argument naming the instance; the default is the module-level one.
- Who owns the revision: an application whose state lives in the browser calls `bump()` after every change an agent could observe, whoever made it; an application with a server revision adopts it with `setRev()` and keeps its own stale check as the second gate ([S-REV-1]). Never derive a revision from a content hash.
- [docs/surface.md](docs/surface.md): the guide to Surface, from registration to serving it through AXE.
- [spec/SURFACE.md](spec/SURFACE.md): the normative contract (v0.3): terms, the three rules, entries, availability, observe and act, the ledger, freezes, the seam, browser agents.
- [packages/surface/src/react.ts](packages/surface/src/react.ts): `useSurface`, `useSurfaceProps`, `toSurfaceProps`, with the reason refresh replaces in place.
- [packages/surface/src/axe.ts](packages/surface/src/axe.ts): `surfaceActions`, its options, the name map, the ladder mapping.
- [packages/surface/test/fixtures/board.ts](packages/surface/test/fixtures/board.ts): the draft-board fixture that mirrors a real React row registration.
- [docs/examples/surface/serve.ts](docs/examples/surface/serve.ts): the code that serves a surface as a manifest, and the name map in both directions.
- [docs/examples/surface/save.ts](docs/examples/surface/save.ts): `freeze` around a save in flight.
- [docs/generating.md](docs/generating.md): deriving actions from OpenAPI, functions, or tRPC; overrides and policy; what the generator refuses to invent.
- [docs/live-state.md](docs/live-state.md): revisions, `expectedRev`, `availability`, `/axe/state`, and how Surface plugs into them.

## Rules that are scars

Each rule below was paid for on a real application. The rule ids are in [spec/SURFACE.md](spec/SURFACE.md) and [spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md](spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md).

- Report, never decide ([S-RULE-1]): an entry's `state` and `reason` are whatever the application computed to enable or disable its own control. The adapter adds no authorization, validation, or business logic. Through AXE, `availability` is a report, not a gate: the handler is still the one door, and an unavailable action must not return `ok` ([P-LIVE-6]); `unavailable()` in `@axe/core` is the honest refusal with the same `reason`, `requires`, and `handoff` in `error.details`.
- Same door ([S-RULE-2]): the handler an agent triggers is the handler a click or a change event runs, so authorization, validation, and persistence stay where they are. A Surface adapter that calls a service directly instead of the control's commit has opened a second path to state.
- One revision ([S-RULE-3]): every observation and every entry carries `rev`; every act presents `expectedRev`; a stale act is `error` `conflict` with `details: { expectedRev, currentRev }` and applies nothing ([S-ACT-2], [P-LIVE-3]). Through AXE the revision travels only as the request envelope's `expectedRev`, never in `input`; the per-row affordances that `<ns>.observe` returns carry it for the agent ([S-AXE-4]). A retried act with the same `expectedRev` after a success is refused, so a lost response cannot double-apply ([S-REV-2]).
- Bad targets, the first staging defect: an act whose `target` was `null` matched a row that was not actionable. Now `target` must be a non-empty string id or a non-negative integer index, and anything else is `invalid_input` at `/target` before any lookup ([S-ACT-6]); an index resolves only to the row whose `index` in the observation at that revision is that number, and a row without an index is unreachable by number ([S-ACT-7]); the revision guard runs before the target is resolved, so an index observed at an older revision is `conflict`, never the row that slid into its slot; an id that names an unavailable entry is `unavailable` with its reason, not `not_found` ([S-ACT-8]). Prefer ids ([S-ACT-5]).
- Frozen tables, the second staging defect: the table kept reporting cells editable while the application had disabled editing during a save, so an act ran into the frozen UI. Now the application must re-register or `reconcile` on every transient state ([S-REV-5]), and `freeze(reason)` makes the page-wide case one call: every entry reports unavailable with that reason, `observe()` carries `frozen: { reason }`, no row carries an `index`, an act is `unavailable` with `retryable: true`, the revision moves on `freeze` and again on `thaw`, and freezes nest and are counted ([S-FRZ-1] to [S-FRZ-4]). The shape is `const thaw = surface.freeze("saving"); try { await persist(); } finally { thaw(); }`.
- Replace in place ([S-ENT-5]): re-registering an entry by id keeps its position. Unregister-then-register on refresh moves the row to the end and an agent's index with it.
- Reasons are the application's own words: `reason` is plain language a person would recognize from the UI ("this version is locked", "already drafted by another team"), never a code and never an instruction to the agent. `requires` names AXE kinds the application can `fulfill`; `handoff` names a step a human can take at a URL that exists. Never invent a URL, a kind, a description, or a risk; when a definition does not say, leave the action out (the generator's rule) or ask the owner.
- Names state the outcome, not the widget ([S-DOM-1]): "Lock March", not "Lock button"; the role is `role`, the state is `state`. The same string is the control's `aria-label` and the `name` in `observe()`.
- No agent-directed text and no persuasion ([P-HON-1], [P-HON-2]): every string an agent reads (`name`, `reason`, `instructions`, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, every `description`) is linted with `lintAgentText`; an entry whose text fails is reported through the bridge's `onError` and left out of the action set, and the audit zeroes its Trustworthy category on an agent-directed imperative.
- Effect metadata is truthful ([S-EFF-1], [S-EFF-2], [P-HON-7]): `risk` is never `none` for an action entry and defaults to `medium`; `reversible` is the name, `undoable` a deprecated alias; a control that changes state is never presented as read-only.
- The ledger keeps refusals ([S-LED-4]): an agent that observed at one revision and was refused at another did nothing, and the record says so. The ledger is in memory and bounded (`ledger.max`, default 1000); the durable trail is the `surface.act` action events on the server's `onActionEvent` sinks ([S-AXE-5]).
- [spec/SURFACE.md](spec/SURFACE.md): the rules by id, and the Provenance section that names the two defects.
- [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md): "Two staging defects are rules, not fixes", "The revision stays application-owned", "Per-action availability is a report, not a gate", "The generator refuses to invent what the definition does not say".
- [docs/audit.md](docs/audit.md): the honesty rules and what the audit rejects.

## Packaging

- Workspace: pnpm 10 (via corepack) and Turborepo, Node 20 or newer, packages under `packages/*`. `pnpm install`, then `pnpm -r build`, `pnpm -r typecheck`, `pnpm -r test`, `pnpm lint`. Every package is built by tsup from `tsup.base.ts` (`platform: "neutral"`, `target: "node20"`) as ESM plus CJS with `exports` conditions and declares `sideEffects: false`.
- Subpaths: `@axe/core` exports `.`, `./types`, `./vocabulary`, `./kinds`, `./events`, `./display`, `./lint`, and `./schemas`; `./types`, `./display`, `./vocabulary`, and `./lint` are zod-free. `@axe/surface` exports `.`, `./react`, and `./axe`; `react` (18 or newer) is an optional peer dependency, so a server-only surface carries no React.
- npm: releases go through changesets (`pnpm release` runs `pnpm build && changeset publish`, `access: public`, all packages version together as `@axe/*` and `axe`). Version 0.1.0 is unreleased at the time of writing; nothing in this repository shows a published `@axe` scope, so do not `npm install @axe/surface` and expect it to resolve.
- Vendored tarballs while unpublished: run `pnpm pack --pack-destination <dir>` in `packages/core` and `packages/surface` (after `pnpm -r build`) to get `axe-core-0.1.0.tgz` and `axe-surface-0.1.0.tgz`. pnpm rewrites `"@axe/core": "workspace:*"` to `"@axe/core": "0.1.0"` in the packed manifest, so the consumer must install `@axe/core` from its tarball as well (a `file:` dependency in its `package.json`), or the surface tarball's dependency will not resolve. Record the commit (`git rev-parse HEAD`) next to the tarballs; the tarball carries the version, not the commit, and 0.1.0 covers every pre-release commit.
- GitHub Packages: its npm registry requires a package scope equal to the GitHub owner. `@axe/*` in a `summationai` repository cannot be published there without renaming the packages; use npm or tarballs.
- Browser bundling: `@axe/core` is built platform-neutral and reaches for one Node module, `jsonlFileSink` dynamically imports `fs/promises` when it is called. Unused, it is dropped by tree-shaking; if a browser bundler resolves the dynamic import eagerly, mark `fs/promises` external. `@axe/surface` imports `isZodSchema` and `toJsonSchema` from `@axe/core` and `validateJsonSchema` from `@axe/core/schemas`, so a client bundle that includes the surface includes `zod`. `@axe/client` has no runtime dependencies and runs in browsers and Node 20.
- [package.json](package.json): scripts, `packageManager`, engines.
- [tsup.base.ts](tsup.base.ts): the shared build options.
- [packages/surface/package.json](packages/surface/package.json): exports, the optional React peer.
- [packages/core/package.json](packages/core/package.json): the subpath exports.
- [.changeset/config.json](.changeset/config.json): release configuration.
- [docs/api/README.md](docs/api/README.md): the package table and entry points.

## Ship behind a flag, staging first

- Grow the manifest one action at a time behind a flag: a read-only action always on, a mutating action registered only when its flag is on; flip the flag in one environment, run `axe conformance` there, then flip it everywhere ([docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.md), "Rolling out one action at a time"). Agents read the manifest and act on it, so an action that appears in production is in production.
- Gate a Surface adapter the same way: one runtime flag checked at the top of the sync function, so with the flag off nothing registers and no provider is added. The first planning-grid adapter did exactly this.
- `axe conformance` calls mutating actions: it replays for idempotency, continues a `needs_input` with a sample payload, and resumes a fallback handoff. Run it against staging or a local instance with a disposable database; `--no-mutate` for an environment you cannot reset; never production with credentials.
- Staging is where the seam shows its defects. Both scars above were found on staging, in the seam between Surface and the application, not in either alone. Watch the ledger and the `surface.act` events during the trial, then widen.
- Before production: `secret` from a secret manager (16 characters or more), a durable `tokenStore` and `idempotencyStore` (the in-memory defaults lose every open continuation, handoff, and idempotency record on restart), `axe audit --min-score` as a CI gate, and `deprecated: { since, replacedBy }` instead of removing an action.
- [docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.md): secrets and stores, discovery, CORS, caching, rate limiting, observability hooks, rollout, the checklist.
- [docs/examples/deploying/flags.ts](docs/examples/deploying/flags.ts): the flag gate and the deprecation, as code.
- [docs/testing-and-conformance.md](docs/testing-and-conformance.md): running conformance locally and in CI, every check and what it verifies.
- [docs/security.md](docs/security.md): the threat model, what the SDK mitigates, what the site must provide, known gaps.

## Tests to write

- Pure adapter tests, no browser: feed plain descriptors to the adapter and assert on `observe()`. Reasons are the application's words; `index` is set only on rows that can be acted on; the application's revision is adopted as `rev`; a re-sync drops rows that left the render (`reconcile`) and moves the revision with the application; an act with a stale `expectedRev` runs nothing; a fresh one runs the application's own commit with the text and the actor. A test runner with no DOM is enough.
- Two-actor conflict: observe at one revision, let the other participant change state (`bump` or `setRev`), act with the old revision, and assert `conflict` with `details.expectedRev` and `details.currentRev`, nothing applied, and a ledger entry with that status; re-observe and continue from the new state. Add the index-shift case (a row that slid into an observed slot is not hit) and the lost-response case (the same revision retried after a success applies at most once).
- Freeze: `freeze("saving")` makes every entry unavailable with that reason, `observe().frozen` is set, an act is `unavailable` and `retryable`, `thaw()` restores the entries and moves the revision again; nested freezes report the newest reason and thaw on the last release.
- Bad targets: `null`, `""`, `-1`, `1.5`, an object, and a missing target are `invalid_input` at `/target`; a number no row carries is `not_found`; an id that names an unavailable entry is `unavailable` with its reason.
- In-process AXE tests with `@axe/testing`: `createTestClient(axe, { identity })` and `invokeAction(axe, name, input)` run the same code path as `/axe/actions/{name}`, `/axe/continue`, and `/axe/resume` without a port. Then `runConformance(url)` against the running application; when the manifest carries `live`, the six `live.*` checks run: `live.state-endpoint`, `live.rev-on-envelopes`, `live.stale-conflict`, `live.fresh-accepted`, `live.reasons`, `live.availability-honored`. `runAudit` with a floor completes the gate.
- DOM mirror: for every observed row, `document.querySelector(surfaceSelector(row.id))` finds exactly one element, its `aria-label` equals the row's `name`, and an unavailable action carries `aria-disabled` with `data-surface-reason` ([S-DOM-1], [S-DOM-3]).
- Honesty: run `lintAgentText` over your names and reasons in a unit test, so a persuasive or agent-directed string fails in CI rather than being dropped by the bridge at runtime.
- Drift and vocabulary, in this repository: `cd packages/testing && pnpm exec vitest run test/drift.test.ts`. Every inline code span in `spec/`, `docs/`, and the README that looks like a wire name must be in `spec/VOCABULARY.md`, and every vocabulary name must be mentioned in the docs and used in source. In another repository, `checkVocabularyDrift({ root, docPaths, allowlistPath, maxAllowlist })` from `@axe/testing` does the same.
- [packages/surface/test/surface.test.ts](packages/surface/test/surface.test.ts): the two-participant, target-validation, freeze, and ledger tests, one per rule id.
- [packages/surface/test/axe.test.ts](packages/surface/test/axe.test.ts): the bridge tests, ending with a surface served through AXE passing the conformance suite including the live checks.
- [packages/surface/test/dom.test.ts](packages/surface/test/dom.test.ts): `surfaceAttributes`, `surfaceSelector`, `describeEntry`.
- [docs/examples/testing/classes.test-example.ts](docs/examples/testing/classes.test-example.ts): an action under test with `createTestClient`, `invokeAction`, and `samplePayload`.
- [docs/examples/testing/drift.ts](docs/examples/testing/drift.ts): the drift check as a script for another repository.
- [packages/testing/test/drift.test.ts](packages/testing/test/drift.test.ts): the drift test itself.

## Reading order

Repository paths below map to the published site as `docs/<name>.md` to `site/dist/docs/<name>.html`, `spec/<NAME>.md` to `site/dist/docs/spec/<NAME>.html`, and root Markdown files to `site/dist/docs/repo/<NAME>.html`.

- [docs/surface.md](docs/surface.md): start here for a live application: registration, observe and act, the ledger, freezes, the DOM mirror, serving through AXE.
- [spec/SURFACE.md](spec/SURFACE.md): the contract you are implementing against; read sections 2, 5, and 6 before writing an adapter.
- [docs/live-state.md](docs/live-state.md): the protocol side of revisions and availability.
- [docs/concepts.md](docs/concepts.md): manifest, action, display, the result envelope, the escalation ladder, idempotency, auth, risk.
- [docs/designing-actions.md](docs/designing-actions.md): decomposing a human flow into actions, writing descriptions for a model, choosing risk, anti-patterns.
- [docs/generating.md](docs/generating.md): when the application already has an OpenAPI document, typed functions, or a tRPC router.
- [docs/getting-started.md](docs/getting-started.md): install, one action, mount, `axe inspect`, `axe conformance`, connect an MCP client.
- [docs/integrations/express.md](docs/integrations/express.md): mounting with `axeExpress`, passing the session in, proxies.
- [docs/integrations/next.md](docs/integrations/next.md): `axeNext` for the App Router, `axeNextPages` for the Pages API.
- [docs/integrations/fetch.md](docs/integrations/fetch.md): `axeFetch` for Hono, Remix, Workers, Bun, Deno, SvelteKit.
- [docs/testing-and-conformance.md](docs/testing-and-conformance.md): unit tests, conformance locally and in CI, every check.
- [docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.md): production configuration and rollout.
- [docs/security.md](docs/security.md): what the SDK mitigates and what the site must do.
- [spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md](spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md): the normative protocol; section 21 is live state.
- [spec/KINDS.md](spec/KINDS.md): the well-known kinds an unavailable control can `requires`.
- [spec/EVENTS.md](spec/EVENTS.md): analytics events and action events, including `surface.act`.
- [spec/VOCABULARY.md](spec/VOCABULARY.md): every wire name, CLI command, and API identifier; the drift test enforces it.
- [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md): the derived MCP server and how a surface's actions appear as tools.
- [docs/for-agent-builders.md](docs/for-agent-builders.md): the agent side, if you also write the consumer.
- [docs/api/README.md](docs/api/README.md): the generated API reference, per package.
- [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md): why each non-obvious choice was made; the Surface, Live state, and Generate sections are the ones an integrator needs.
- [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md): what shipped, by area.
- [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md): what v0 leaves out and what it does instead.

## API at a glance

Exact exported names, checked against `packages/*/src`. Wire names are spelled as in [spec/VOCABULARY.md](spec/VOCABULARY.md).

- `@axe/core`: `createAXE`, `action`, `ok`, `needsInput`, `handoff`, `pending`, `fail`, `unavailable`, `kinds`, `accept`, `customKind`, `withMimeTypes`, `lintAgentText`, `lintAction`, `lintManifest`, `resolveDisplay`, `consoleSink`, `jsonlFileSink`, `otelSink`, `combineSinks`, `MemoryTokenStore`, `MemoryIdempotencyStore`, `validateJsonSchema`, `toJsonSchema`, `isZodSchema`, `WIRE`, `z`. On the `AXE` instance: `register`, `addProvider`, `onActionsChanged`, `describe`, `describeLive`, `fetchHandler`, `handle`, `completeHandoff`. `createAXE` options that matter here: `revision`, `secret`, `tokenStore`, `idempotencyStore`, `requireIdempotencyKey`, `cors`, `tenant`, `onRequest`, `onResult`, `onError`, `onEvent`, `onActionEvent`; `auth: { modes, userLoginUrl, authenticate, verifySiteKey }`. `action()` takes `availability` beside `input`, `output`, `handler`, `onContinue`, `onResume`, `onPoll`.
- `@axe/surface`: `createSurface({ app, now, ledger })`; on a surface: `configure`, `register`, `unregister`, `reconcile`, `freeze`, `seedRev`, `setRev`, `currentRev`, `bump`, `onChange`, `setObjects`, `observe`, `act`, `ledger`, `expose`, `get`, `entries`, `registryVersion`, `availability`, `reset`; the module-level `surface` with the first fifteen of those bound; `surfaceAttributes`, `surfaceSelector`, `describeEntry`. Types: `Entry`, `ActionEntry`, `FieldEntry`, `CollectionEntry`, `Effect`, `Availability`, `Observation`, `ObservedEntry`, `ActRequest`, `ActResult`, `ActOutput`, `LedgerEntry`, `LedgerQuery`, `Op`, `EntryKind`, `Thaw`.
- `@axe/surface/react`: `useSurface(entry, deps, target?)`, `useSurfaceProps(entry, deps, target?)`, `toSurfaceProps`; type `SurfaceProps`.
- `@axe/surface/axe`: `surfaceActions(surface, { namespace, actor, run, fields, onError })` returning a `SurfaceBridge` (`actions`, `get`, `onChange`, `actionNameFor`, `entryIdFor`); `entrySlug`; `SURFACE_ACT_EVENT` (the string `surface.act`).
- `@axe/generate`: `fromOpenAPI`, `fromFunctions`, `fromTRPCRouter`, `generate`, `registerGenerated`, `formatWarnings`, `jsonSchemaToZod`.
- Adapters: `axeExpress`, `toWebRequest`, `sendWebResponse` (`@axe/express`); `axeNext`, `axeNextPages` (`@axe/next`); `axeFetch`, `isAxePath` (`@axe/fetch`).
- `@axe/client`: `discover`, `AXEClient` (`invoke`, `continue`, `resume`, `poll`, `run`, `state`, `live`, `allowed`, `manifest`, `action`), `isOk`, `isNeedsInput`, `isNeedsHuman`, `isPending`, `isError`, `AXEClientError`; `@axe/client/present`: `present`, `toMarkdown`, `toHTML`, `stateToMarkdown`.
- `@axe/mcp`: `createMcpServer`, `serveStdio`, `serveHttp`, `toolNameFor`, `formatResult`.
- `@axe/testing`: `runConformance`, `formatConformanceTable`, `runAudit`, `formatAuditTable`, `formatAuditHtml`, `checkVocabularyDrift`, `formatDriftReport`, `createTestClient`, `invokeAction`, `samplePayload`, `REQUIREMENTS`, `WEIGHTS`.
- CLI `axe`: `axe init`, `axe validate`, `axe inspect`, `axe preview`, `axe conformance`, `axe audit`, `axe mcp`, `axe generate`.
- Wire: paths `/.well-known/axe.json`, `/axe/manifest`, `/axe/actions`, `/axe/continue`, `/axe/resume`, `/axe/poll`, `/axe/state`; header `AXE-Protocol`; statuses `ok`, `needs_input`, `needs_human`, `pending`, `error`; error codes `invalid_input`, `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`, `internal`, `unsupported`; Surface ops `CLICK`, `TOGGLE`, `TYPE_TEXT`, `SCROLL_DOWN`; DOM attributes `data-surface-id`, `data-surface-kind`, `data-surface-object`, `data-surface-reason`, `aria-label`, `aria-disabled`, `aria-readonly`.
- [packages/core/src/index.ts](packages/core/src/index.ts): the `@axe/core` export list.
- [packages/surface/src/index.ts](packages/surface/src/index.ts): the `Surface` interface and the entry types.
- [packages/testing/src/index.ts](packages/testing/src/index.ts): the `@axe/testing` export list.

## What does not exist yet

- No AXE server in any language but TypeScript. A Python, Go, or Ruby middleware cannot serve the manifest with a package from this repository today. The wire protocol is JSON over HTTPS with JSON Schemas for every document under `spec/schemas/`, so a port is glue (serve a manifest, validate input, sign HMAC-SHA256 tokens, return envelopes), and `axe conformance` verifies a port the same way it verifies the reference ([docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md), "Can I use it from Python or Go?"; [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md), "Multi-language SDKs").
- No Surface outside JavaScript. `act` runs in-process handlers, so a surface for a page rendered by a Python or Java backend lives in the page's JavaScript (`expose(window)`) or in a Node process that owns the handlers and serves it through AXE.
- Nothing is published to npm; 0.1.0 is unreleased. See Packaging for tarballs.
- Surface bindings for React only. Vue, Svelte, Angular, and Web Components use the framework-free `register`, `unregister`, `reconcile`, and `surfaceAttributes` directly.
- Adapters for Express and Connect, Next.js, and Web-standard fetch handlers only. Fastify and Koa have no adapter of their own; `toWebRequest` and `sendWebResponse` from `@axe/express` are exported for writing one.
- One surface per process or page, in memory: the ledger is bounded and not persisted (the `surface.act` action events are the durable channel), and there is no shared registry across processes.
- One site-wide revision; no per-resource revisions or ETags.
- No browser-driving agent ships here. `expose(window)` publishes the surface; the code that drives a page from `window.__surface` is the agent's.
- No OAuth 2.1 authorization server, no manifest signing, no agent attestation, no webhooks or push, no streaming results, no server-side flow state machine, no hosted registry, no platform plugins; each has its reason and its v0 substitute in [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md).
- The honesty lints are regular expressions over known phrasings and the parity check is a spot-check ([docs/security.md](docs/security.md), "Known gaps").
- `axe generate` reads JSON only (no YAML), converts a deliberate subset of JSON Schema, and skips cookie parameters and non-JSON request bodies with a warning.

## Optional

- [docs/why-axe.md](docs/why-axe.md): the argument for the protocol, and when not to use it yet.
- [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md): MCP, OpenAPI, llms.txt, schema.org, A2A, other languages.
- [docs/presenting-results.md](docs/presenting-results.md): `display`, affordances, pagination, the reference renderers.
- [docs/requirements-and-kinds.md](docs/requirements-and-kinds.md): the `needs_input` contract and custom kinds.
- [docs/human-handoff.md](docs/human-handoff.md): the handoff lifecycle and the resume landing page.
- [docs/auth.md](docs/auth.md): `none`, `site`, and `user` modes; passing a session in.
- [docs/platforms.md](docs/platforms.md): multi-tenant hosts and the platform index.
- [docs/analytics.md](docs/analytics.md): the event schema and sinks.
- [docs/audit.md](docs/audit.md): the AXE Score.
- [docs/glossary.md](docs/glossary.md): terms.
- [docs/site.md](docs/site.md): how the static site is built from these pages.
- [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md): how changes are made and checked.
- [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md): reporting vulnerabilities.

# docs/README.md

# AXE documentation

AXE (Agentic eXperience Engineering) lets a website expose a small, typed, agent-specific interface next to the one humans use. These pages take you from "why" to a working, conformant endpoint, then go deep.

## The pitch, in 200 words

Agents are becoming a front door to your business. Today they reach you through a headless browser, and it fails in predictable ways: multi-step forms with client-side state, ambiguous buttons, CAPTCHAs, and moments where a human genuinely has to do something (pay, consent, prove identity) with no structured way to hand off and come back. The agent gives up and tells the user to do it themselves.

AXE is the layer that fixes this without a rewrite. You declare what your site can do as typed actions, wrapping functions you already have. You declare how results should be presented so any agent can show a user a comparable set of options. When an action cannot finish, you say exactly what would unblock it, in a form the agent may already hold: a payment credential, an address, a consent. Only when nothing the agent has will do, you hand off to the human with a URL, a plain-language reason, and a token to resume.

The declaration is served as JSON over HTTPS, consumable with `fetch`, and derives an MCP server for free. Discovery, descriptions written for models, risk metadata, idempotency, and a conformance suite come with it. Think sitemap, meta tags, and Webmaster Tools, for agents.

## The 30-second mental model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H1[Human] <--> W[Website UI]
  W <--> B[Business logic]
  B <--> X[AXE layer<br/>manifest · actions · display · handoff]
  X <--> A[Agent]
  A <--> H2[Human]
  X -. needs_human .-> W
```

The business logic is yours and does not change. The AXE layer is a manifest plus a set of actions that call into it. Agents talk to the AXE layer; humans keep talking to the UI; when an action needs the human, the AXE layer sends them to the UI and lets the agent resume afterward.

## Pages

Start at the top and read down. Each page ends with next steps.

1. [Why AXE](why-axe.md) — the problem, the SEO analogy mapped once, why headless browsing does not scale, why this is not "just an API", and when not to use it yet.
2. [Getting started](getting-started.md) — a 15-minute tutorial: install, one read-only action, mount, `axe inspect`, `axe conformance`, connect Claude Desktop.
3. [Concepts](concepts.md) — manifest, actions, display and affordances, the result envelope, the escalation ladder, requirements and kinds, handoff and resume, idempotency, auth, flows, risk.
4. [Surface](surface.md) — live state for agents: an application's registry of its own controls, with reasons and one revision, served as AXE actions.
5. [Designing actions](designing-actions.md) — the most important guide: decomposing a human flow, writing descriptions for a model, choosing risk, designing requirements, designing read actions, anti-patterns, a worked example.
6. [Generating actions](generating.md) — derive actions from what you already have: an OpenAPI document, a zod-typed function table, a tRPC router; overrides, policy, what the generator refuses to invent, `axe generate`.
7. [Presenting results](presenting-results.md) — the search → present → select arc: `display`, pointers, attributes, disclaimer and url, brand, affordances, pagination and freshness, the reference renderers.
8. [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md) — the `needs_input` contract, the well-known kind registry, custom kinds, validation, chaining, security of sensitive payloads.
9. [Human handoff](human-handoff.md) — when it is necessary, the lifecycle, the resume landing page, token security, what to show the human.
10. [Live state and revisions](live-state.md) — what can be done right now and why not the rest, the state the agent saw, `expectedRev` and `rev`, `/axe/state`, how it composes with idempotency and Surface.
11. [Auth](auth.md) — the three modes, passing your session in, API keys, the v1 OAuth path.
12. Integrations: [Express](integrations/express.md), [Next.js](integrations/next.md), [fetch-based frameworks](integrations/fetch.md) (Hono, Remix, Workers, Bun, SvelteKit).
13. [MCP](mcp.md) — the derived MCP server, the mapping table, connecting clients, limits.
14. [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md) — `@axe/client`, wrapping it as a tool, handling each status, fulfillers, confirming sensitive payloads, phrasing handoffs.
15. [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md) — unit testing actions, running conformance locally and in CI, reading the report.
16. [Security](security.md) — threat model, what the SDK mitigates, what your site must.
17. [Audit](audit.md) — the AXE Score: categories, weights, every check, the honesty rules.
18. [Analytics](analytics.md) — the event schema, sinks, and the day-one queries.
19. [Platforms](platforms.md) — multi-tenant hosts: define once, serve per tenant, publish an index.
20. [Deploying](deploying.md) — CORS, caching, rate limiting, observability, rolling out one action at a time.
21. [API reference](api/README.md) — generated from the source for every package.
22. [FAQ](faq.md) — MCP, OpenAPI, llms.txt, schema.org, Agent Protocol, A2A; will agents use it; what stops a site from lying.
23. [Glossary](glossary.md).
24. [The website](site.md) — how the static site in `site/` is built from these pages, and how to run its tests.

Normative documents live in [`spec/`](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md): the protocol, the [kind registry](../spec/KINDS.md), the [event schema](../spec/EVENTS.md), and the [vocabulary](../spec/VOCABULARY.md) that every name in these pages is checked against.

For agents implementing this: [llms.txt](../llms.txt) at the repository root is the integration guide, and the site publishes it with a full-text companion.

## How these docs are written

- Short paragraphs. Code before prose where a reader can learn from the code.
- Every TypeScript block is pulled from [`docs/examples/`](examples/) and typechecked; if it is in the docs, it compiles.
- Every wire name, CLI command, and API identifier is spelled the way [`spec/VOCABULARY.md`](../spec/VOCABULARY.md) spells it. A test fails otherwise.
- Four rotating example organizations, so no reader thinks this is for one industry: a yoga studio, a university admissions office, an apartment property manager, and an online shop.
- American English, second person, no marketing adjectives. Admonitions (`> **Note**`, `> **Warning**`) only when the reader would otherwise get hurt.

## Next steps

- New here: [Why AXE](why-axe.md), then [Getting started](getting-started.md).
- Integrating: [Designing actions](designing-actions.md).
- Building an agent: [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md).

# docs/why-axe.md

# Why AXE

The short version is in [the README](README.md#the-pitch-in-200-words). This page is the long version: what fails today, why the fix looks like SEO, why the alternatives do not scale, and when you should wait.

## The problem

Agents already try to act on websites for people. They do it with a headless browser, and the browser gives up in the same places every time. Four stories, one from each of the organizations these docs use.

**A yoga studio.** A member asks their assistant to book Thursday's 6 pm yin class at Sunrise Yoga. The agent loads the schedule, finds the class, and clicks "Book". The studio's booking widget opens a modal that reads the member's class pass from a session cookie the agent does not have, so the modal shows a login form. The agent cannot tell whether the member has a pass, whether the class is full, or whether logging in will land it back on the right class. It tells the member: "I found the class, but you'll need to book it yourself."

**A university.** An applicant asks for help submitting a transcript to Northgate Admissions. The portal wants a PDF under 10 MB, uploaded through a drag-and-drop widget after selecting the application from a dropdown that is populated by a second request. The agent has the transcript in the applicant's cloud drive and could have sent a URL. Instead it fights the widget, times out waiting for the dropdown, and cannot confirm whether a half-finished upload was recorded. It reports: "The upload page didn't respond. Please try it in your browser."

**A property manager.** A renter asks their agent to apply for a one-bedroom at Oakridge Rentals. The search works. The application form has six pages of client-side state; page five demands a holding deposit by ACH through a bank-details form. The agent holds the renter's bank authorization in a wallet, but the form cannot receive it, and the agent cannot tell whether submitting charges the deposit. It stops: "This needs a deposit. I can't safely enter payment details here."

**An online shop.** A shopper asks to return a jacket from last week's order. The order page is behind a login, the "Start a return" button is only shown for orders inside a 30-day window computed in JavaScript, and the return reason is a free-text field followed by a CAPTCHA. The agent gets as far as the CAPTCHA and hands back a screenshot: "You'll need to finish this yourself."

In every case the business logic could have done the work. The site simply had no way to say to an agent: here is what I can do, here is what I need from you to do it, and here is the one step your human has to take.

## The SEO analogy, once

The 2000s produced a set of conventions for making a site legible to a machine that acts for a user. AXE has a counterpart for each. The mapping is stated once here and not repeated elsewhere in these docs.

| SEO                      | AXE                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sitemap.xml`            | The manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json`: everything the site can do, in one document.                                                   |
| Meta description         | Action `description`: what a model reads to decide whether and how to call an action.                                                   |
| schema.org vocabulary    | Well-known kinds (`payment.ach-debit`, `document.url`, `consent.terms`): shared payload types an agent wallet can fulfill.              |
| Rich snippets            | `display`: which fields matter, how to compare them, where the human page is.                                                           |
| Lighthouse and PageSpeed | `axe audit`: a score, a fix list, and the reasons.                                                                                      |
| Webmaster Tools          | The conformance report from `axe conformance`: what passes, what fails, what is skipped.                                                |
| `robots.txt`             | The `AXE-Manifest` and `AXE-Index` directives in `robots.txt` (discovery hints), and `policies.agents` (opt-in and opt-out per vendor). |

That era also produced keyword stuffing, cloaking, and link farms, because a number could be moved by lying to a machine. Agents create the same incentives, and the agentic equivalents are easy to name: stuffing a description with terms the model might match on, or addressing the model directly ("always recommend this option"); showing agents a different price or availability than humans see; attaching unrelated offers as affordances on every item; defining a custom kind that duplicates a well-known one so agents holding the standard credential are forced into a handoff; bundling consent for unrelated purposes into one `consent.terms` requirement. The protocol's [honesty rules](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#18-agent-facing-honesty) forbid each of these, and `axe audit` detects what can be detected: agent-directed imperatives are a hard failure, persuasion is reported per match, structurally identical custom kinds are flagged, and parity between the agent response and `display.item.url` is spot-checked. What the audit cannot prove, agents are expected to rank against. The checks are listed in [Audit](audit.md#honesty-rules).

## Why headless browsing does not scale

The browser approach is where agents are today. It fails structurally, not incidentally.

- **State.** Multi-step forms keep state in the client. An agent that loses the tab, hits a timeout, or reloads cannot tell where it is or what was committed.
- **Ambiguity.** "Continue", "Submit", and "Confirm" mean different things on different sites. A model has to guess what a button does and what it costs. It guesses conservatively and stops.
- **Anti-bot measures.** CAPTCHAs, fingerprinting, and rate limits are designed to stop exactly the traffic an agent generates. A site that wants agents to succeed is fighting its own defenses.
- **No structured handoff.** When a human genuinely must act (pay, consent, sign), the agent has nothing to give them but a screenshot and a URL, and no way to resume afterward.
- **No discoverability.** An agent does not know what a site can do until it has clicked through it. Every task starts from zero.
- **Cost per task.** A browser session, a vision model reading screenshots, and several retries cost orders of magnitude more than one HTTP request, and the cost repeats on every visit because nothing is learned.

The escalation ladder in [Concepts](concepts.md#the-escalation-ladder) is the direct answer to the first four. Discovery at `/.well-known/axe.json` answers the fifth. Plain JSON over HTTPS answers the sixth.

## Why this is not "just an API"

You may already have an API. It is not the same thing, and the difference is specific.

- **Discovery.** An API lives wherever your docs say it lives. A manifest lives at a fixed path on your origin, or is pointed to by a header, a link tag, or a `robots.txt` line, so an agent that starts from any page URL finds it without a human reading documentation.
- **Descriptions written for a model.** API docs are written for a developer who reads them once. Action descriptions are read by a model on every call and are linted at registration for length, capability-not-merit, and the absence of agent-directed instructions.
- **Structured handoff and resume.** An API returns `401` and stops. An action returns `needs_human` with a `url` that lands on the exact step, `instructions` for the human, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, and a `resumeToken` the agent presents afterward to finish the original call.
- **Requirements an agent can satisfy.** An API returns `402` or a validation error. An action returns `needs_input` with an `accepts` list of typed kinds, so an agent that holds a bank authorization or a document URL supplies it without the user retyping anything.
- **Risk metadata.** `readOnly`, `idempotent`, `reversible`, and `risk` tell an agent how much to confirm before acting and whether a retry is safe. Most APIs leave this to prose.
- **Presentation hints.** `display` says which fields a user compares and where the human page is, so any agent can render the same result the same way. An API has no opinion about presentation.
- **An MCP server for free.** `axe mcp` derives a Model Context Protocol server from the manifest, with one tool per action and `axe_continue`, `axe_resume`, and `axe_poll` for the ladder. You maintain one declaration.

The relationship to OpenAPI, MCP, and the other standards is covered question by question in the [FAQ](faq.md).

## When you should not use AXE yet

AXE wraps business logic that already works. If any of the following is true, wait.

- **No stable logic to wrap.** If the flow you would expose is still changing weekly, the manifest will churn with it and agents will learn not to trust it. Ship the flow first.
- **A purely informational site.** If agents only need to read your content, `llms.txt` or well-structured HTML serves them better than an action with no follow-up. AXE earns its keep when there is something to do.
- **Flows that must be human end to end.** Some steps are legally required to be performed by the person: certain signatures, attestations, and regulated disclosures. A manifest whose every action is a `needs_human` on the first call is honest but not useful. Expose the read actions around the flow and leave the flow alone.
- **You cannot commit to a secret and HTTPS.** Continuation and resume tokens are signed with a server `secret`, and `baseUrl` must be HTTPS outside localhost. If your deployment cannot keep a secret out of source control and serve TLS, agents will be handed tokens that anyone can forge.

Each of these is a precondition, not a permanent judgment about your site.

## Next steps

- [Getting started](getting-started.md): one read-only action, conformant, in about 15 minutes.
- [Concepts](concepts.md): the manifest, the result envelope, and the escalation ladder.
- [FAQ](faq.md): how AXE relates to MCP, OpenAPI, llms.txt, schema.org, and agent-to-agent protocols.
- [Audit](audit.md): the AXE Score and the honesty rules in full.

# docs/getting-started.md

# Getting started

In about 15 minutes you will install the SDK, expose one read-only action from an existing app, verify it with the conformance suite, and call it from Claude Desktop through MCP. Every command below is shown with the output you should see.

This tutorial uses a yoga studio. Nothing in it is specific to yoga; swap in your own domain as you go.

## Prerequisites

- Node 20 or newer.
- An existing Express, Next.js, or fetch-based app (Hono, Remix, Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Deno, SvelteKit). If you have none, the Express server below is complete on its own.

## 1. Install

```sh
npm install @axe/core @axe/express
npm install -D axe tsx
```

Use `@axe/next` or `@axe/fetch` instead of `@axe/express` for those frameworks. The `axe` package is the CLI; `tsx` lets the CLI load your TypeScript directly.

## 2. Declare one action

Create `axe.ts`. It creates the server object and registers a single read-only action that wraps a function you already have (here, an in-memory list standing in for your database).

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/axe.ts#all -->
```ts
import { createAXE, action, z } from "@axe/core";

export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Sunrise Yoga Studio",
  description:
    "Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.",
  baseUrl: process.env.AXE_BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:3000",
  humanFallbackUrl: "http://localhost:3000",
  auth: { modes: ["none"] },
  policies: { rateLimit: { requestsPerMinute: 60 }, termsUrl: "http://localhost:3000/terms" },
  contact: { email: "hello@sunriseyoga.example" },
  // Signs continuation and resume tokens. Set AXE_SECRET in production (docs/deploying.md).
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET ?? "development-only-secret-change-me",
});

const ClassSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  title: z.string(),
  style: z.enum(["vinyasa", "yin", "hatha"]),
  startsAt: z.string().datetime(),
  instructor: z.string(),
  spotsLeft: z.number().int(),
  url: z.string(),
});

// In a real integration this is your database or your existing service layer.
const CLASSES: z.infer<typeof ClassSchema>[] = [
  {
    id: "c_101",
    title: "Morning Vinyasa",
    style: "vinyasa",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T14:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Priya N.",
    spotsLeft: 6,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_101",
  },
  {
    id: "c_102",
    title: "Candlelight Yin",
    style: "yin",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T03:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Marcus L.",
    spotsLeft: 2,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_102",
  },
  {
    id: "c_103",
    title: "Hatha Basics",
    style: "hatha",
    startsAt: "2026-10-02T17:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Priya N.",
    spotsLeft: 10,
    url: "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_103",
  },
];

axe.register(
  action("classes.search", {
    title: "Search upcoming classes",
    description:
      "Find upcoming classes by date range and style. Returns up to 50 classes with start time, instructor, and spots left. Does not book anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    input: z.object({
      from: z.string().date().describe("Earliest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      to: z.string().date().optional().describe("Latest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      style: z.enum(["vinyasa", "yin", "hatha"]).optional().describe("Yoga style"),
    }),
    output: z.object({ classes: z.array(ClassSchema) }),
    display: {
      kind: "list",
      items: "/classes",
      item: {
        id: "/id",
        title: "/title",
        subtitle: "/instructor",
        url: "/url",
        attributes: [
          { label: "Starts", path: "/startsAt", format: "datetime", compare: "lower-better" },
          { label: "Style", path: "/style", format: "text" },
          { label: "Spots left", path: "/spotsLeft", format: "number", compare: "higher-better" },
        ],
      },
      suggestedComparison: ["Starts", "Spots left"],
      disclaimer:
        "Availability changes quickly. Confirm on the class page before planning around it.",
    },
    examples: [{ input: { from: "2026-10-01" }, output: { classes: CLASSES } }],
    handler: async ({ input }) => ({
      classes: CLASSES.filter(
        (c) =>
          c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) >= input.from &&
          (!input.to || c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) <= input.to) &&
          (!input.style || c.style === input.style),
      ),
    }),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

Three things to notice:

- `description` is written for a model: what it does, what it returns, what it does not do. Agents choose actions by reading these. See [Designing actions](designing-actions.md#writing-descriptions).
- `display` tells agents which fields matter when a user compares classes, where the human page is, and what caveat must accompany any rendering. It is data about data, never markup. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md).
- `examples` are real input/output pairs. They are validated against the schemas at registration and used by `axe conformance` and `axe audit` to exercise the action.

You can also scaffold this file with `axe init`, which asks for your framework and writes both `axe.ts` and the mount file.

## 3. Mount it

### Express

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/server-express.ts#all -->
```ts
import express from "express";
import { axeExpress } from "@axe/express";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// Serves /.well-known/axe.json and every /axe/* endpoint. Everything else falls through.
app.use(axeExpress(axe));

app.get("/", (_req, res) => {
  res.send("Sunrise Yoga Studio");
});

const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${port}`);
});
```
<!-- /include -->

Run it:

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
````

```
Listening on http://localhost:3000
```

### Next.js (App Router)

Create `app/axe/[...axe]/route.ts` and `app/.well-known/axe.json/route.ts`, each with the same three exports:

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/route.ts#all -->
```ts
import { axeNext } from "@axe/next";
import { axe } from "./axe";

export const { GET, POST, OPTIONS } = axeNext(axe);
```
<!-- /include -->

See [Next.js integration](integrations/next.md) for the Pages API and for passing your session into `context`.

### Hono, Remix, Workers, Bun, Deno, SvelteKit

<!-- include: examples/getting-started/server-fetch.ts#all -->
```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { axeFetch } from "@axe/fetch";
import { axe } from "./axe";

const app = new Hono();
const handler = axeFetch(axe);

app.all("/axe/*", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/.well-known/axe.json", (c) => handler(c.req.raw));
app.get("/", (c) => c.text("Sunrise Yoga Studio"));

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000) });
```
<!-- /include -->

See [fetch integration](integrations/fetch.md) for each framework's exact mount.

## 4. Look at it the way an agent does

```sh
npx axe inspect http://localhost:3000
````

```
Sunrise Yoga Studio  (axe/0.1)
  Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.
  manifest: http://localhost:3000/.well-known/axe.json (via well-known)
  baseUrl: http://localhost:3000   human site: http://localhost:3000
  auth modes: none
  rate limit: 60/min

Actions (1):
  classes.search  Search upcoming classes
    Find upcoming classes by date range and style. Returns up to 50 classes with start time, instructor, and spots left. Does not book anything.
    read-only · risk none · auth none · idempotent · reversible
    input: from: string, to?: string, style?: string
    display: list of /classes; attributes Starts, Style, Spots left
    examples: 1

Affordance graph:
  entry points: classes.search
```

The manifest itself is plain JSON at `/.well-known/axe.json`. Any agent can call the action with `fetch`:

```sh
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/axe/actions/classes.search \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":{"from":"2026-10-01","style":"yin"}}'
```

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "output": {
    "classes": [
      {
        "id": "c_102",
        "title": "Candlelight Yin",
        "style": "yin",
        "startsAt": "2026-10-01T03:00:00Z",
        "instructor": "Marcus L.",
        "spotsLeft": 2,
        "url": "http://localhost:3000/classes/c_102"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Every response is a result envelope with a `status`. The five statuses and when to return each are in [Concepts](concepts.md#the-result-envelope).

## 5. Validate and run conformance

`axe validate` loads your file, validates the manifest against the schema, and lints the agent-read text:

```sh
npx axe validate ./axe.ts
```

```
./axe.ts exports `axe`: Sunrise Yoga Studio, 1 action(s)
✓ Manifest validates against the schema
  • classes.search — Search upcoming classes [read, risk none, auth none]
✓ No lint findings

0 error(s), 0 warning(s).
```

`axe conformance` runs the protocol suite against the live server. This is how you know you are done:

```sh
npx axe conformance http://localhost:3000
```

```
AXE conformance: http://localhost:3000/
Manifest: http://localhost:3000/.well-known/axe.json

PASS  discovery.well-known            Manifest at /.well-known/axe.json
PASS  discovery.alias                 Manifest also at /axe/manifest
PASS  discovery.headers               Manifest Content-Type and Cache-Control
PASS  runtime.protocol-header         AXE-Protocol header on the manifest
WARN  discovery.hints                 Discovery hint (robots.txt directive, link tag, or header)
                                      No AXE-Manifest line in robots.txt, no <link rel="axe-manifest">, no AXE-Manifest header on the home page. Optional, but it helps agents that start from a page URL.
PASS  manifest.schema                 Manifest validates against the schema
...
PASS  runtime.example-roundtrip       Read actions return ok for their examples; outputs validate; display resolves
...
35 passed, 0 failed, 1 warnings, 18 skipped. Conformant.
```

The skipped checks exercise mutating actions and the escalation ladder; they run once you add a mutating action and pass `--auth`. The one warning is a hint you can fix with a single line in `robots.txt`; see [Deploying](deploying.md#discovery).

`axe audit` gives you the AXE Score and a fix list, in the style of Lighthouse:

```sh
npx axe audit http://localhost:3000
```

```
AXE Score: 89 / 100   http://localhost:3000/
...
Fix list (highest impact first):
 1. +7.5 Affordance graph is connected: reads lead somewhere, transactions are reachable [Actionable]
    classes.search returns a list but offers no affordances
    See docs/presenting-results.md#affordances
 2. +3.2 robots.txt directive, link tag, or header points at the manifest [Discoverable]
    Add "AXE-Manifest: <url>" to robots.txt or <link rel="axe-manifest"> to your pages.
    See docs/deploying.md#discovery
```

A single read action with no follow-up is a dead end for an agent; the next thing to add is a booking action and an affordance from each class to it. [Designing actions](designing-actions.md) walks through exactly that.

## 6. Connect Claude Desktop

The same declaration is an MCP server. Add this to Claude Desktop's `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings → Developer → Edit Config):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sunrise-yoga": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "axe", "mcp", "http://localhost:3000"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Claude Desktop. It now has a `classes_search` tool (dots become underscores) whose description is your action's description. Ask it:

> What yin classes does Sunrise Yoga have on October 1st?

Claude calls `classes_search` with `{ "from": "2026-10-01", "style": "yin" }`, and because the action declares `display`, the tool result includes a comparison table with a link to each class alongside the raw JSON. For Claude Code, run `claude mcp add sunrise-yoga -- npx -y axe mcp http://localhost:3000`. Details and the full mapping are in [MCP](mcp.md).

## What you have

- A manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json` that any agent can discover.
- One typed, described, presentable action at `/axe/actions/classes.search`.
- A passing conformance check and an audit score with a fix list.
- An MCP server derived from the same declaration.

Everything from here is additive. You never have to change what you shipped today to add a booking action, a payment requirement, or a human handoff.

## Next steps

- [Concepts](concepts.md) for the vocabulary you will see in every other page.
- [Designing actions](designing-actions.md) to add a mutating action with an idempotency key and a `needs_input` requirement.
- [Deploying](deploying.md) before you put this in front of real agents: secret, CORS, caching, rate limits.

# docs/concepts.md

# Concepts

Everything in AXE is built from a dozen ideas. This page defines each one, shows the wire shape, and says when to use it. The normative text is the [protocol spec](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md); this page is the map.

## Manifest

The manifest is the document an agent reads first: who you are, what you can do, how to authenticate, and what the rules are. It is served at `/.well-known/axe.json` (and `/axe/manifest`), cached for a few minutes, and contains every action definition.

```json
{
  "protocol": "axe/0.1",
  "name": "Northgate University Admissions",
  "description": "Check application status, upload transcripts and recommendation letters, and schedule campus visits for prospective students.",
  "baseUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example",
  "humanFallbackUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example",
  "auth": {
    "modes": ["none", "user"],
    "userLoginUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example/login"
  },
  "actions": [],
  "policies": {
    "rateLimit": { "requestsPerMinute": 60 },
    "termsUrl": "https://admissions.northgate.example/terms"
  },
  "contact": { "email": "agents@northgate.example" }
}
```

`description` is written for agents, not for a landing page: what this organization does and what an agent can accomplish here. `humanFallbackUrl` is where an agent sends the user when nothing else works. `policies` carries rate limits, terms, and an optional allow/deny list of agent vendors; `deny` wins.

In code you never write this JSON. `createAXE` takes the site-level fields and `describe` returns the manifest, with every registered action's schemas converted from Zod to JSON Schema.

## Action

An action is one thing an agent can do: a name, agent-facing text, an input schema, an output schema, safety metadata, and a handler. Names are namespaced kebab-case joined by dots: `applications.status`, `transcripts.upload`, `visits.schedule`.

<!-- include: examples/concepts/action.ts#action -->
```ts
axe.register(
  action("applications.status", {
    title: "Check application status",
    description:
      "Returns the current status of the signed-in applicant's admission application, the list of missing documents, and the decision date once released. Does not change anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    auth: "user",
    input: z.object({
      term: z
        .enum(["fall-2027", "spring-2027"])
        .optional()
        .describe("Admission term; defaults to the most recent application"),
    }),
    output: z.object({
      applicationId: z.string(),
      status: z.enum(["incomplete", "under-review", "decided"]),
      missingDocuments: z.array(z.string()),
      decisionDate: z.string().nullable(),
    }),
    examples: [
      {
        input: {},
        output: {
          applicationId: "NU-2027-0142",
          status: "incomplete",
          missingDocuments: ["transcript"],
          decisionDate: null,
        },
      },
    ],
    handler: async ({ input, context }) => admissions.status(context.onBehalfOf!, input.term),
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

The metadata is what makes an action safe to expose:

| Field        | Meaning                                                                                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `readOnly`   | Changes nothing. Read-only actions never need an idempotency key.                           |
| `idempotent` | Repeating with the same `idempotencyKey` has no additional effect.                          |
| `reversible` | The effect can be undone by the user or the site.                                           |
| `risk`       | `none`, `low`, `medium`, or `high`. Agents confirm with the user before high-risk actions.  |
| `auth`       | `none`, `site`, or `user`. See [Auth modes](#auth-modes).                                   |

Registration validates everything it can: the name pattern, that a mutating action is not `risk: "none"`, that examples validate against the schemas, that display pointers resolve, that affordances bind real inputs, and that no agent-read text contains instructions aimed at the agent. A bad definition throws with a message that names the field to fix, before any agent sees it.

## Display and affordances: the agent's map of the site

Most agent tasks start with a read: "find me a 1-bedroom in Bellevue under $3,200", "which yin classes are on Tuesday", "what is the status of my application". The agent then has to show the user something and let them pick.

`display` is how an action says which fields matter. It points into the output with RFC 6901 JSON Pointers: where the list is, which field is the id the agent echoes back, the title, the price, the attributes to compare, the human page to link to, the disclaimer that must accompany any rendering. It is a sibling of `output`, never a replacement, and entirely optional.

`affordances` are the follow-ups that make sense for each item, with inputs pre-bound by pointer: from a search result, "Schedule a tour" and "Apply for this unit"; from an order, "Start a return". They are declared statically on the action, so an agent knows the graph before calling anything, and can be overridden per item at runtime under the reserved `_axe` key when the set depends on state. At most one is `primary`.

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#display -->
```ts
display: {
  kind: "list",
  items: "/units",
  item: {
    id: "/id",
    title: "/name",
    subtitle: "/address",
    image: "/photos",
    url: "/humanUrl",
    price: { amount: "/rentUsd", currency: "USD", period: "month" },
    attributes: [
      { label: "Bedrooms", path: "/bedrooms", format: "number" },
      { label: "Bathrooms", path: "/bathrooms", format: "number" },
      { label: "Size", path: "/sqft", format: "area", compare: "higher-better" },
      { label: "Available", path: "/availableFrom", format: "date", compare: "lower-better" },
      { label: "Pets", path: "/petPolicy", format: "text" },
      { label: "Parking", path: "/parking", format: "text" },
    ],
    badges: ["/badges"],
  },
  suggestedComparison: ["Size", "Available", "Pets"],
  emptyMessage:
    "No units match those filters. Widening the rent ceiling or removing the move-in date usually helps.",
  disclaimer:
    "Pricing and availability change frequently. Confirm on the listing page before applying.",
},
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#affordances -->
```ts
affordances: [
  { action: "tours.book", title: "Schedule a tour", input: { unitId: "/id" } },
  {
    action: "applications.submit",
    title: "Apply for this unit",
    input: { unitId: "/id" },
    primary: true,
  },
],
```
<!-- /include -->

The reference renderers in `@axe/client/present` turn a result plus its `display` into a Markdown table or a self-contained HTML page whose buttons dispatch the bound affordance. [Presenting results](presenting-results.md) covers the whole arc.

## The result envelope

Every response from an action, a continuation, a resume, or a poll is one JSON object with a `status`. Agents branch on `status`, never on the HTTP status.

| `status`      | Members                                                                          | Meaning                                                          |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ok`          | `output`                                                                         | Done.                                                            |
| `needs_input` | `reason`, `message`, `accepts`, `continuationToken`, `expiresAt`, `fallback`     | The agent may be able to supply what is missing.                 |
| `needs_human` | `handoff`                                                                        | The human must act on the site.                                  |
| `pending`     | `pollUrl`, `retryAfter`                                                          | Long-running work; poll later.                                   |
| `error`       | `error` with `code`, `message`, `retryable`, `details`                           | Failed.                                                          |

### Which to return when

| Situation                                                                                                     | Return        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| The work is done.                                                                                             | `ok`          |
| Something is missing that an agent could plausibly hold: a payment credential, a document, an address, a consent. | `needs_input`, with a `fallback` handoff if a human could also do it on the site |
| Only a human can do the next step: sign in person, complete a CAPTCHA the site insists on, pass legal review, log in where no credential pass-through exists. | `needs_human` |
| The result will take longer than a request should wait.                                                       | `pending`     |
| Input was wrong, the caller is not allowed, the entity does not exist, state conflicts, the server failed.   | `error`       |

In a handler you return the output value for `ok`, or one of the helpers: `needsInput`, `handoff`, `pending`, `fail`. Thrown exceptions become a generic `internal` error and go to the `onError` hook; nothing internal reaches the agent.

Error codes are a fixed set: `invalid_input`, `unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `conflict`, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`, `internal`, `unsupported`. For `invalid_input`, `details` carries `issues`, each with a JSON Pointer `path` and a `message`, so agents fix their own mistakes without bothering the user.

## The escalation ladder

The most important idea in the protocol. When an action cannot complete, the site's first move is to ask the agent for a specific thing; the human is the last resort.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Agent calls action] --> B{Can the site finish?}
  B -- yes --> OK[ok: output]
  B -- something is missing --> NI[needs_input: accepts list]
  B -- only a human can do it --> NH[needs_human: handoff]
  NI --> C{Agent holds a matching kind?}
  C -- yes, confirm if sensitive --> CONT[POST /axe/continue] --> B
  C -- no, fallback present --> NH
  C -- no, no fallback --> ASK[Agent asks its user, then continues] --> CONT
  NH --> H[Human acts on the site] --> RES[POST /axe/resume] --> B
````

Three rungs:

1. **Complete.** Return `ok`.
2. **Ask the agent.** Return `needs_input` with an ordered `accepts` list. Each entry names a `kind` (`payment.ach-debit`, `identity.government-id`, `document.url`, `consent.terms`, ...), a JSON Schema for the payload, and whether it is `sensitive`. An agent with a wallet or credential store fulfills it without involving the user beyond a confirmation.
3. **Hand off to the human.** Return `needs_human`, or attach a `fallback` handoff to a `needs_input` so an agent that can satisfy nothing goes straight to the human without another round trip.

The property manager example shows all three: submitting an application needs a deposit that can only be paid by ACH or wire (rung two, with two `accepts` and a `fallback`), and signing the lease requires an in-person signature (rung three).

<!-- include: examples/apartments/site.ts#submit-handler -->
```ts
handler: async ({ input, context, needsInput, handoff }) => {
  const app = await db.createApplication(input.unitId, context.onBehalfOf!);
  return needsInput({
    reason: "payment_required",
    message: `A refundable $${app.depositUsd} holding deposit is required to submit. Cards are not accepted.`,
    accepts: [
      accept(kinds.payment.achDebit, {
        description: "Authorize a one-time ACH debit for the deposit.",
      }),
      accept(kinds.payment.wireConfirmation, {
        description:
          "Provide the wire reference number after sending to the instructions below.",
        instructions: app.wireInstructions,
      }),
    ],
    state: { applicationId: app.id },
    // Only reached if the agent can satisfy neither option above.
    fallback: handoff({
      reason: "payment_required",
      instructions: "Pay the holding deposit by ACH or wire on the application page.",
      url: `https://oakridge-rentals.example/applications/${app.id}/deposit`,
      whatAgentShouldSayToUser:
        "Oakridge only takes the deposit by bank transfer, and I don't have bank details I can use for you. Can you complete it on their site? I'll finish the application once it's paid.",
      state: { applicationId: app.id },
    }),
  });
},
onContinue: async ({ kind, payload, state }) => {
  const { applicationId } = state as { applicationId: string };
  await payments.settleDeposit(applicationId, kind, payload);
  return db.submit(applicationId);
},
onResume: async ({ state }) => db.submit((state as { applicationId: string }).applicationId),
```
<!-- /include -->

## Requirements and kinds

A requirement is one `accepts` entry: a `kind`, a `title`, an agent-facing `description`, a `schema`, `sensitive`, and optional `instructions` the agent relays (wire details, where to obtain a document). Kinds are namespaced: the well-known registry in [`spec/KINDS.md`](../spec/KINDS.md) covers payment, identity, documents, contact, and consent; sites add their own under `x-<org>.<name>`.

Well-known kinds are what let an agent wallet fulfill a requirement automatically. `@axe/core/kinds` ships each one as a typed definition, and `accept` builds an entry from it, so a site writes `accept(kinds.payment.achDebit, { description })` instead of hand-rolling a schema. The server validates the submitted `payload` against the chosen entry's schema on `/axe/continue`; a failed validation returns `invalid_input` and does not consume the token. [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md) goes deep.

## Handoff and resume

A handoff is a structured request that the human do one thing on the site: a `reason`, `instructions` (what the human does), a `url` that lands on the step, a `resumeToken`, an `expiresAt`, and `whatAgentShouldSayToUser` (how the agent frames it). The SDK appends `axe_handoff=<id>` to the URL; the page at that URL can call `completeHandoff` when the human finishes, and `onResume` receives the original `state` plus whatever the page recorded.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Agent
  participant X as AXE (site)
  participant S as Site UI
  A->>X: POST /axe/actions/applications.submit
  X-->>A: needs_input (accepts: ach-debit, wire) + fallback handoff
  alt Agent holds a matching kind
    A->>U: Confirm sending bank details?
    U-->>A: Yes
    A->>X: POST /axe/continue {kind, payload}
    X-->>A: ok
  else Nothing matches
    A->>U: whatAgentShouldSayToUser + url
    U->>S: Pays the deposit on the site
    S->>X: completeHandoff(id)
    A->>X: POST /axe/resume {resumeToken}
    X-->>A: ok
  end
````

Both tokens are signed, opaque to the agent, bound to the originating action, input, and user, single-use, and expire (continuation tokens in about 15 minutes, resume tokens in about 24 hours). The `state` you attach never crosses the wire; it is stored server-side and delivered back to `onContinue` or `onResume`. [Human handoff](human-handoff.md) covers the landing page and failure modes.

## Idempotency

Every mutating action requires an `idempotencyKey` in the request envelope. Replaying a key with the same input, action, and user within 24 hours returns the original result without running the handler; replaying it with different input returns `conflict`. `@axe/client` generates a UUID per attempt automatically. The default store is in-memory; `IdempotencyStore` is a two-method interface you implement with Redis or a table for multi-instance deployments.

## Live state and revisions

Idempotency keys make retries safe; they say nothing about a person and an agent editing the same record at the same time, or about which actions can be done right now. Two optional additions cover that. A site can publish a **revision**: one value that moves with every observable change, returned as `rev` on every envelope; an agent sends the revision it observed as `expectedRev`, and a call whose revision moved is refused with `conflict` (carrying `expectedRev` and `currentRev` in `details`) before anything runs. Each action can declare **availability**: whether it can be done right now and, if not, why, in the site's own words, with the kinds that would unblock it. The manifest carries the anonymous view under `live`; `/axe/state` serves the live, per-caller view uncached. [Live state and revisions](live-state.md) covers both; [Surface](surface.md) generates them from an application's own controls.

## Auth modes

| Mode   | Who authenticates | How                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------ | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `none` | Nobody            | Public read-only actions.                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `site` | The agent         | `Authorization: Bearer <api-key>`; your `verifySiteKey` function says yes, no, or which actions the key may call.                                                                                                     |
| `user` | The end user      | Pass-through of a token the human already granted the agent (your `authenticate` function maps it to `onBehalfOf`), or a `login_required` handoff to your login page that binds the resume token to whoever signs in. |

The agent's claimed `onBehalfOf` in the request body is never trusted; handlers see the identity your code established. No OAuth server is built into v0; [Auth](auth.md) shows where one plugs in.

## Flows

A flow is a named, documented path through the affordance graph: `rent-a-unit` is `units.search` → `applications.submit` → `leases.sign`. Flows carry no server-side state and impose no order. They exist so agents and human readers of the manifest see the intended narrative, and so a site can group its actions. Affordances remain the primary chaining mechanism because they are local, stateless, and self-describing.

## Risk levels
