        .latencyMs, .kind, .errorCode, .tenant, .schemaVersion] | @csv' axe-events.jsonl > axe-events.csv

psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "\copy axe_events (ts, action, status, ladder, agent_vendor, agent_name, agent_version, latency_ms, kind, error_code, tenant, schema_version) FROM 'axe-events.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv)"
```

Rotate the file with your log rotation and ship it the way you ship other logs. The sink appends; it does not rotate.

## What is deliberately not in the events

Rule [E-2] of the spec lists what an event must never contain: `input`, `output`, `payload`, `state`, tokens, `onBehalfOf`, `sessionId`, IP addresses, or any header value other than the parsed agent fields. The SDK enforces this by giving the event type no place to put them. You can add sinks freely, export events to a third party, and give analysts access to the table, because the table cannot contain a deposit amount, a transcript, or a user id.

The cost is that events alone cannot answer "what did this user do" or "which input produced this error". When you need that, correlate in your own logs, on your own terms:

- Read your request id from the request in `onRequest` and `onResult`, and log it with the action and status. The [Observability hooks](deploying.md#observability-hooks) section shows the wiring.
- Keep that request id, and anything derived from it, out of the AXE event. Do not wrap a sink to append it. The point of the separation is that the events table stays safe to share.
- If you log input for debugging, redact payloads of `sensitive` kinds before the log line is written. The SDK validates a payment or identity payload against its schema and passes it to `onContinue`; it never logs it, and neither should you. [Security](security.md) covers this in detail.

## Next steps

- [Deploying](deploying.md): the hooks, rate limiting, and rollout steps that produce the events you query here.
- [Designing actions](designing-actions.md): what to change when the handoff rate or the `invalid_input` rate is high.
- [Platforms](platforms.md): serving many tenants from one deployment, and what `tenant` means on the events.
- [Event spec](../spec/EVENTS.md): the normative shape and rules.

# docs/platforms.md

# Platforms

A platform hosts many sites on one codebase: a scheduling product with ten thousand studios, a storefront builder, a university system with forty campuses. Every site runs the same code with different data, a different domain, and a different name on the door. AXE treats that shape as a first-class case: you declare actions once, a resolver says which tenant a request belongs to, and every tenant gets its own manifest at its own domain.

This page uses StudioHost, a class-scheduling platform whose tenants include Sunrise Yoga Studio, Moon Pilates, and River Barre. The full example is [`docs/examples/platforms/platform.ts`](examples/platforms/platform.ts).

## One integration, every site

A single studio adopting AXE puts one site in front of agents. A platform adopting it puts every site it hosts in front of agents in the same deploy, with the same action set, the same conformance result, and the same audit fixes. The studios do nothing; they were never going to write an integration, and they do not have to. For agents, a platform index is the difference between finding one manifest and finding ten thousand.

The declaration does not change shape. `createAXE` takes the same fields it takes for a single site, plus a `tenant` resolver and an `index`. Handlers receive the resolved tenant and scope their queries by it. That is the whole platform surface. Platform plugins for specific hosts are on the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md); the multi-tenant core described here is what they will be built on.

## Define actions once

Actions are never per tenant. Sunrise Yoga and Moon Pilates both expose `classes.search`, because they both run StudioHost's scheduler. What differs between them is data, and data is scoped inside the handler.

Start with the per-tenant overlay. A `TenantInfo` carries only the fields that differ between studios: the stable `id` that appears on every event, the `name`, the `baseUrl` at the studio's own domain, and optional overrides for the manifest fields covered in [Serve per-tenant manifests](#serve-per-tenant-manifests).

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#tenants -->
```ts
// Stand-ins for your tenants table and your class schedule.
interface Studio {
  id: string;
  host: string;
  name: string;
  description: string;
  accentColor: string;
  requestsPerMinute: number;
  deniedVendors: string[];
  updatedAt: string;
}
const studios: Studio[] = [
  {
    id: "st_101",
    host: "sunriseyoga.example",
    name: "Sunrise Yoga Studio",
    description:
      "Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.",
    accentColor: "#e0a458",
    requestsPerMinute: 60,
    deniedVendors: [],
    updatedAt: "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
  },
  {
    id: "st_102",
    host: "moonpilates.example",
    name: "Moon Pilates",
    description:
      "Find reformer and mat Pilates sessions by date and level, check equipment availability, and reserve a reformer once signed in.",
    accentColor: "#3b3f8f",
    requestsPerMinute: 30,
    deniedVendors: ["scraperco"],
    updatedAt: "2026-09-12T00:00:00Z",
  },
  {
    id: "st_103",
    host: "riverbarre.example",
    name: "River Barre",
    description:
      "Browse barre classes by date and instructor, see spots left, and book or join a waitlist once signed in.",
    accentColor: "#2f7a5a",
    requestsPerMinute: 60,
    deniedVendors: [],
    updatedAt: "2026-08-20T00:00:00Z",
  },
];
const db = {
  async studioByHost(host: string) {
    return studios.find((s) => s.host === host) ?? null;
  },
  async allStudios() {
    return studios;
  },
  // One page of studios for the index. `page` is the cursor from the previous page's `next`.
  async studiosPage(page: string | null, size: number) {
    const start = page ? Number(page) : 0;
    const slice = studios.slice(start, start + size);
    const next = start + size < studios.length ? String(start + size) : null;
    return { studios: slice, next };
  },
  async searchClasses(studioId: string, filters: { from: string; to?: string | undefined }) {
    return SCHEDULE.filter(
      (c) =>
        c.studioId === studioId &&
        c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) >= filters.from &&
        (!filters.to || c.startsAt.slice(0, 10) <= filters.to),
    );
  },
};
const SCHEDULE = [
  {
    studioId: "st_101",
    id: "c_101",
    title: "Morning Vinyasa",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T14:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Priya N.",
    spotsLeft: 6,
    url: "https://sunriseyoga.example/classes/c_101",
  },
  {
    studioId: "st_102",
    id: "c_201",
    title: "Reformer Level 1",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T16:00:00Z",
    instructor: "Dana K.",
    spotsLeft: 3,
    url: "https://moonpilates.example/classes/c_201",
  },
  {
    studioId: "st_103",
    id: "c_301",
    title: "Barre Fundamentals",
    startsAt: "2026-10-01T17:30:00Z",
    instructor: "Lena O.",
    spotsLeft: 8,
    url: "https://riverbarre.example/classes/c_301",
  },
];

// A tenant is the per-studio overlay on the shared declaration: the fields that differ
// between studios, and nothing else. Actions are never per tenant.
function tenantInfo(studio: Studio): TenantInfo {
  const baseUrl = `https://${studio.host}`;
  return {
    id: studio.id,
    name: studio.name,
    baseUrl,
    description: studio.description,
    humanFallbackUrl: baseUrl,
    brand: { name: studio.name, accentColor: studio.accentColor, tone: "casual" },
    policies: {
      rateLimit: { requestsPerMinute: studio.requestsPerMinute },
      termsUrl: `${baseUrl}/terms`,
      ...(studio.deniedVendors.length > 0 ? { agents: { deny: studio.deniedVendors } } : {}),
    },
    contact: { email: `hello@${studio.host}` },
    auth: { userLoginUrl: `${baseUrl}/login` },
    indexUrl: "https://studiohost.example/.well-known/axe-index.json",
    updatedAt: studio.updatedAt,
  };
}
```
<!-- /include -->

The resolver runs once per request and maps the request to a tenant, or to none. Resolve by hostname when tenants have their own domains or subdomains; that is the natural fit, because each tenant's manifest then sits at `/.well-known/axe.json` on its own origin.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#resolver -->
```ts
// Called once per request. Returning null makes every endpoint answer not_found for
// that host, and no manifest is served there. The index is the one exception.
async function resolveTenant(request: Request): Promise<TenantInfo | null> {
  const host = new URL(request.url).hostname;
  const studio = await db.studioByHost(host);
  if (!studio || !enabledForAgents(studio)) return null;
  return tenantInfo(studio);
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Pass the resolver to `createAXE`. The platform-level `name`, `description`, and `baseUrl` describe the platform itself; a tenant overrides each of them.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#create -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  // Platform-level values. A tenant overrides each of these; the platform's own host
  // (studiohost.example) resolves to no tenant and serves only the index.
  name: "StudioHost",
  description:
    "Class scheduling for independent fitness studios. Each studio publishes its own manifest at its own domain; this platform publishes the index of them.",
  baseUrl: "https://studiohost.example",
  humanFallbackUrl: "https://studiohost.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none", "user"] },
  policies: { rateLimit: { requestsPerMinute: 60 }, termsUrl: "https://studiohost.example/terms" },
  contact: { email: "agents@studiohost.example" },
  tenant: resolveTenant,
  index,
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
});
```
<!-- /include -->

Every handler, `onContinue`, `onResume`, and `onPoll` receives `tenant` alongside `input` and `context`. Scope every query by the tenant's `id`. Tokens and idempotency keys are already bound to the tenant by the SDK, so a continuation minted on one studio's domain cannot be replayed on another's, but row-level isolation inside your data layer is yours to enforce.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#handler -->
```ts
const ClassSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  title: z.string(),
  startsAt: z.string().datetime(),
  instructor: z.string(),
  spotsLeft: z.number().int(),
  url: z.string(),
});

axe.register(
  action("classes.search", {
    title: "Search upcoming classes",
    description:
      "Find this studio's upcoming classes by date range. Returns up to 50 classes with start time, instructor, spots left, and a link to the class page. Does not book anything.",
    readOnly: true,
    risk: "none",
    input: z.object({
      from: z.string().date().describe("Earliest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
      to: z.string().date().optional().describe("Latest class date, YYYY-MM-DD"),
    }),
    output: z.object({ classes: z.array(ClassSchema) }),
    display: {
      kind: "list",
      items: "/classes",
      item: {
        id: "/id",
        title: "/title",
        subtitle: "/instructor",
        url: "/url",
        attributes: [
          { label: "Starts", path: "/startsAt", format: "datetime", compare: "lower-better" },
          { label: "Spots left", path: "/spotsLeft", format: "number", compare: "higher-better" },
        ],
      },
      disclaimer:
        "Availability changes quickly. Confirm on the class page before planning around it.",
    },
    examples: [
      {
        input: { from: "2026-10-01" },
        output: {
          classes: [
            {
              id: "c_101",
              title: "Morning Vinyasa",
              startsAt: "2026-10-01T14:00:00Z",
              instructor: "Priya N.",
              spotsLeft: 6,
              url: "https://sunriseyoga.example/classes/c_101",
            },
          ],
        },
      },
    ],
    // Every handler receives the resolved tenant. Scope every query by tenant.id, and
    // never let an id from one studio's input reach another studio's rows.
    handler: async ({ input, tenant, fail }) => {
      if (!tenant)
        return fail("unavailable", "This action is only served on a studio's own domain.");
      const classes = await db.searchClasses(tenant.id, input);
      return { classes: classes.map(({ studioId: _studioId, ...c }) => c) };
    },
  }),
);
```
<!-- /include -->

If tenants live under path prefixes on one host rather than on their own hostnames, resolve the tenant from the path in your framework, rewrite the URL to strip the prefix before it reaches the adapter, and set the tenant's `baseUrl` to include the prefix so the URLs the SDK mints (`pollUrl`, handoff `url` defaults) are correct. The SDK strips only the platform-level `baseUrl` path in v0. A prefixed manifest is not at a well-known location, so agents find it through the index or a discovery hint rather than by convention.

## Serve per-tenant manifests

With a resolver in place, a request for `/.well-known/axe.json` on a tenant's host returns that tenant's manifest. The SDK merges the `TenantInfo` over the platform config field by field: `name`, `baseUrl`, `description`, `humanFallbackUrl`, `brand`, `policies`, `contact`, `indexUrl`, `updatedAt`, and `auth.userLoginUrl` (and `auth.modes`, if you set it). Everything else, above all `actions` and `flows`, is shared. A host the resolver does not recognize gets `not_found` from every endpoint and no manifest at all.

Two studios' manifests differ only in those fields:

```jsonc
// https://sunriseyoga.example/.well-known/axe.json
{
  "protocol": "axe/0.1",
  "name": "Sunrise Yoga Studio",
  "description": "Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.",
  "baseUrl": "https://sunriseyoga.example",
  "humanFallbackUrl": "https://sunriseyoga.example",
  "auth": { "modes": ["none", "user"], "userLoginUrl": "https://sunriseyoga.example/login" },
  "actions": [ /* identical on every tenant */ ],
  "policies": { "rateLimit": { "requestsPerMinute": 60 }, "termsUrl": "https://sunriseyoga.example/terms" },
  "contact": { "email": "hello@sunriseyoga.example" },
  "brand": { "name": "Sunrise Yoga Studio", "accentColor": "#e0a458", "tone": "casual" },
  "indexUrl": "https://studiohost.example/.well-known/axe-index.json",
  "updatedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"
}
````

```jsonc
// https://moonpilates.example/.well-known/axe.json
{
  "protocol": "axe/0.1",
  "name": "Moon Pilates",
  "description": "Find reformer and mat Pilates sessions by date and level, check equipment availability, and reserve a reformer once signed in.",
  "baseUrl": "https://moonpilates.example",
  "humanFallbackUrl": "https://moonpilates.example",
  "auth": { "modes": ["none", "user"], "userLoginUrl": "https://moonpilates.example/login" },
  "actions": [/* identical on every tenant */],
  "policies": {
    "rateLimit": { "requestsPerMinute": 30 },
    "termsUrl": "https://moonpilates.example/terms",
    "agents": { "deny": ["scraperco"] },
  },
  "contact": { "email": "hello@moonpilates.example" },
  "brand": { "name": "Moon Pilates", "accentColor": "#3b3f8f", "tone": "casual" },
  "indexUrl": "https://studiohost.example/.well-known/axe-index.json",
  "updatedAt": "2026-09-12T00:00:00Z",
}
```

Each tenant's `description` is agent-read text and is subject to the [honesty rules](audit.md#honesty-rules) like any other. If tenants write their own, run them through `lintAgentText` before saving, and give them the same guidance as [Writing descriptions](designing-actions.md#writing-descriptions).

For static generation, `describe` takes a `TenantInfo` and returns the manifest the live endpoint would serve. Build one per enabled tenant at deploy time and publish it at that tenant's domain from your CDN, with `Content-Type: application/json` and a `Cache-Control` header of at least 60 seconds.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#describe -->
```ts
// Static generation: build every enabled studio's manifest at deploy time and publish
// each one at its own domain. The output is exactly what the live endpoint serves.
export async function manifestsForAllTenants(): Promise<Map<string, Manifest>> {
  const out = new Map<string, Manifest>();
  for (const studio of await db.allStudios()) {
    if (!enabledForAgents(studio)) continue;
    out.set(studio.host, axe.describe(tenantInfo(studio)));
  }
  return out;
}
```
<!-- /include -->

## Publish axe-index.json

The index is how an agent finds every tenant without a directory. It is a paginated list of manifest URLs served at `/.well-known/axe-index.json` on the platform's own origin. Configure it with `index: { platform, sites }`; `sites` returns one page per call.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#index -->
```ts
// Served at /.well-known/axe-index.json on the platform's origin. One page per call;
// `page` is whatever the previous page put in `next`, or null for the first page.
const index: IndexConfig = {
  platform: { name: "StudioHost", url: "https://studiohost.example" },
  sites: async (page) => {
    const { studios, next } = await db.studiosPage(page, 1000);
    return {
      sites: studios.filter(enabledForAgents).map((s) => ({
        name: s.name,
        manifestUrl: `https://${s.host}/.well-known/axe.json`,
        updatedAt: s.updatedAt,
        tags: ["fitness", "scheduling"],
      })),
      next,
    };
  },
};
```
<!-- /include -->

The wire document:

```json
{
  "protocol": "axe/0.1",
  "platform": { "name": "StudioHost", "url": "https://studiohost.example" },
  "sites": [
    { "name": "Sunrise Yoga Studio", "manifestUrl": "https://sunriseyoga.example/.well-known/axe.json", "updatedAt": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z", "tags": ["fitness", "scheduling"] },
    { "name": "Moon Pilates", "manifestUrl": "https://moonpilates.example/.well-known/axe.json", "updatedAt": "2026-09-12T00:00:00Z", "tags": ["fitness", "scheduling"] }
  ],
  "next": "https://studiohost.example/.well-known/axe-index.json?page=2"
}
````

Four rules from [spec §3.3](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#33-platform-index):

- Keep each page to at most 1000 sites. The SDK builds the `next` URL from the platform `baseUrl` and the cursor you return; agents follow `next` until it is absent.
- Every `manifestUrl` is absolute, and the manifest it resolves to has a `baseUrl` on the same origin. Tenants serve their own manifest at their own domain; the index only points there. A platform that proxies every tenant's manifest from one host violates this rule.
- Each tenant manifest carries `indexUrl` pointing back at the index, so an agent that finds one studio can find the rest.
- Add `AXE-Index: https://studiohost.example/.well-known/axe-index.json` to the platform's `robots.txt`. It is a hint for crawlers, not access control.

The index is exempt from the tenant rule: the platform's own host resolves to no tenant, and the index is still served there. Fetching the index emits no event.

## Per-tenant brand and policies

`brand` gives renderers a name, a logo, an accent color, and a tone per tenant, so a comparison page for Moon Pilates does not look like one for River Barre. Agents treat these as hints; `accentColor` is a CSS hex color, `logoUrl` is absolute HTTPS. See [spec §13.2](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#132-brand-hints).

`policies.agents` is per tenant. A studio that wants to refuse a specific agent vendor puts it in `deny`, matched case-insensitively against `context.agent.vendor`; the SDK enforces the tenant's list (falling back to the platform's) by answering `forbidden`, and agents are required not to call a site that denies them in the first place.

`policies.rateLimit` is per tenant too, and it is a declaration. Moon Pilates declares 30 requests per minute above; nothing in the SDK counts requests. Enforce the limit at your edge, keyed by tenant and vendor, and return `Retry-After` on `429`. The `RateLimit-Policy` header the SDK emits reflects the platform-level `policies.rateLimit`, not the tenant's, in v0. See [Rate limiting](deploying.md#rate-limiting).

## Rollout strategy

Ship to a cohort before you ship to everyone. The resolver is the switch: return `null` for tenants not yet enabled, and they have no manifest and no endpoints, exactly as if the platform had never integrated.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#pilot -->
```ts
// Rollout gate. Start with a named cohort; flip to "everyone" when the pilot is clean.
const PILOT_COHORT = new Set(["st_101", "st_102"]);
const ROLLOUT: "pilot" | "everyone" = "pilot";

function enabledForAgents(studio: Studio): boolean {
  return ROLLOUT === "everyone" || PILOT_COHORT.has(studio.id);
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Then, in order:

1. Run `axe conformance https://sunriseyoga.example` and `axe audit https://sunriseyoga.example` against a pilot tenant's real domain. Conformance is per origin; a platform is conformant when each tenant is. Fix the audit list once and every tenant inherits the fix.
2. Watch events by `tenant`. Every event carries the tenant `id`; the [analytics](analytics.md) queries group by it, so you see per-studio handoff rates and error rates before the studios do.
3. Widen the cohort. Because tenants share one action set, the second thousand tenants behave like the first two.
4. Change actions by deprecating, never by removing. A removed action breaks every tenant at once; a `deprecated` action with `replacedBy` keeps working while agents move. See [Deprecating actions](designing-actions.md#deprecating-actions).

## How a tenant opts out

A manifest is an invitation, and a tenant can decline it in two ways.

The first is total: the resolver returns `null` for that tenant. No manifest is served at its domain, every endpoint answers `not_found`, and the tenant is left out of the index. Store the choice next to the tenant record and read it in the resolver, the same way the pilot gate does.

The second is selective: the tenant's `policies.agents` denies specific vendors, or allows only named ones. The manifest stays up for everyone else. Per [spec §3.4](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#34-opting-out), agents must not call actions on a site whose policy denies their vendor, and the SDK also refuses them with `forbidden`. `deny` wins over `allow`.

Standard `robots.txt` rules apply to the human site and say nothing about AXE endpoints; an opt-out belongs in the resolver or in `policies.agents`, not in a crawl directive.

## Adapter plumbing

If your framework already resolved the tenant before the request reaches AXE, pass it through the adapter's `context` option as `AdapterContext.tenant` rather than looking it up twice. Every adapter accepts the same shape; the Express form is below, and `axeNext` and `axeFetch` take an equivalent function.

<!-- include: examples/platforms/platform.ts#adapter -->
```ts
interface StudioRequest extends NodeRequestLike {
  studio?: Studio | null;
}

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// Your existing middleware already knows which studio a request is for.
app.use(async (req, _res, next) => {
  (req as StudioRequest).studio = await db.studioByHost(req.hostname);
  next();
});

// Pass it through the adapter context instead of resolving twice. When the context
// supplies no tenant, the server falls back to the resolver above, so unknown hosts
// still get not_found.
app.use(
  axeExpress(axe, {
    context: async (req) => {
      const studio = (req as StudioRequest).studio;
      return { tenant: studio && enabledForAgents(studio) ? tenantInfo(studio) : null };
    },
  }),
);

app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
```
<!-- /include -->

Precedence matters. A tenant supplied by the adapter wins. When the adapter supplies none, the server calls the resolver from `createAXE`; only when that also returns `null` does the host get `not_found`. If you configure no resolver and the adapter returns `null`, the request is served as the platform itself, with the platform-level manifest. Keep the resolver configured even when the adapter normally supplies the tenant, so an unknown host cannot fall through to it.

## Next steps

- [Deploying](deploying.md) for CORS, manifest caching, rate limiting, and the stores you need across many instances.
- [Analytics](analytics.md) for the event schema and queries grouped by `tenant`.
- [Audit](audit.md) for the AXE Score you will run against each pilot tenant.
- [Protocol spec §3](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#3-discovery) for the normative index and opt-out rules.
````

# docs/deploying.md

# Deploying

[Getting started](getting-started.md) leaves you with a conformant endpoint on localhost. This page is what changes between that and production: where the secret and the stores live, how agents find you, which headers the SDK emits and which it does not, and how to roll actions out one at a time without breaking the agents that already depend on you.

## Secrets and stores

The SDK signs continuation, resume, and poll tokens with an HMAC over `secret`. It must be at least 16 characters and should come from your secret manager. When it is absent the server logs a warning and generates a random per-process secret, which is fine on a laptop and wrong everywhere else: tokens minted before a restart fail to verify after it, and two instances behind a load balancer cannot verify each other's tokens. Rotating the secret has the same effect on purpose: every outstanding token becomes invalid, so rotate during a quiet period or accept that in-flight handoffs return `not_found` and agents start over.

Tokens carry no state. What the server remembers about an open requirement or handoff lives in a `TokenStore`; the results of mutating calls live in an `IdempotencyStore`, keyed by tenant, action, acting user, and `idempotencyKey`. Both default to in-memory implementations that are correct for one process and silently wrong for two. A Redis-style client with three commands covers both:

<!-- include: examples/deploying/stores.ts#kv -->
```ts
// The subset of a Redis-style client the stores need. ioredis and node-redis both have this shape.
interface KV {
  get(k: string): Promise<string | null>;
  set(k: string, v: string, mode: "EX", ttl: number): Promise<unknown>;
  del(k: string): Promise<unknown>;
}
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/deploying/stores.ts#stores -->
```ts
export function kvTokenStore(kv: KV, prefix = "axe:token:"): TokenStore {
  return {
    async get(id) {
      const raw = await kv.get(prefix + id);
      return raw ? (JSON.parse(raw) as TokenRecord) : undefined;
    },
    async set(id, record, ttlSeconds) {
      await kv.set(prefix + id, JSON.stringify(record), "EX", Math.max(1, Math.ceil(ttlSeconds)));
    },
    async delete(id) {
      await kv.del(prefix + id);
    },
  };
}

export function kvIdempotencyStore(kv: KV, prefix = "axe:idem:"): IdempotencyStore {
  return {
    async get(key) {
      const raw = await kv.get(prefix + key);
      return raw ? (JSON.parse(raw) as IdempotencyRecord) : undefined;
    },
    async set(key, record, ttlSeconds) {
      await kv.set(prefix + key, JSON.stringify(record), "EX", Math.max(1, Math.ceil(ttlSeconds)));
    },
  };
}
```
<!-- /include -->

The SDK passes a TTL on every write: about 15 minutes for continuation tokens, 24 hours for resume tokens, one hour for poll tokens, and the idempotency window (24 hours by default) for idempotency records. Honor it: a store that ignores TTLs grows without bound, and one that shortens them makes handoffs fail before the human gets back.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/stores.ts#config -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Oakridge Rentals",
  description:
    "Search available apartments, schedule tours, and submit rental applications with a holding deposit.",
  baseUrl: "https://oakridge-rentals.example",
  humanFallbackUrl: "https://oakridge-rentals.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none", "user"], userLoginUrl: "https://oakridge-rentals.example/login" },
  // At least 16 characters, from your secret manager. Rotating it invalidates outstanding tokens.
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
  tokenStore: kvTokenStore(kv),
  idempotencyStore: kvIdempotencyStore(kv),
  // The idempotency window. Default 24 hours; the store receives it as the TTL on every record.
  idempotencyTtlSeconds: 60 * 60 * 24,
});
```
<!-- /include -->

The same configuration can disable the `idempotencyKey` requirement. Do not: [idempotency](concepts.md#idempotency) is what makes a retried deposit one deposit.

## Discovery

An agent that has only your home page URL needs to find the manifest. The protocol gives it four places to look, in order, and the SDK serves the first two:

1. `/.well-known/axe.json` at the origin of `baseUrl`. This is the primary location and it must be reachable there, even when `baseUrl` carries a path prefix.
2. `/axe/manifest`, an alias for hosts that cannot serve anything under `.well-known`.
3. The `AXE-Manifest` response header on any page of your site, carrying the absolute manifest URL. Add it at your web server or CDN; the SDK does not emit it because it does not serve your pages.
4. A `<link rel="axe-manifest" href="...">` element in the `<head>` of your HTML.

For crawlers, `robots.txt` may carry two lines:

````

AXE-Manifest: https://www.oakridge-rentals.example/.well-known/axe.json
AXE-Index: https://www.oakridge-rentals.example/.well-known/axe-index.json

````

The second is for [platforms](platforms.md) that publish an index of tenant manifests. Both lines are hints, not access control; an agent that skips `robots.txt` still finds the manifest at the well-known path. To refuse an agent, use `policies.agents`: a `deny` list of vendor names, or an `allow` list that permits only the vendors it names. Deny wins, matching is case-insensitive, and the SDK returns `forbidden` to a denied vendor.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/production.ts#policies -->
```ts
policies: {
  rateLimit: { requestsPerMinute: 120, burst: 30 },
  termsUrl: "https://www.oakridge-rentals.example/agent-terms",
  dataRetention: "Application data is kept for 12 months after the last activity.",
  // Deny wins. An absent allow list permits every vendor that is not denied.
  agents: { deny: ["scraper-co"] },
},
```
<!-- /include -->

`axe conformance` warns when it finds no hint beyond the well-known path, and `axe audit` awards points for one. The cheapest fix is the `robots.txt` line.

## CORS

CORS is off unless you turn it on, and when it is off the SDK emits no CORS headers at all. `OPTIONS` requests still get a `204` with an `Allow` header, so a health check does not mistake the endpoint for dead.

Enable it only for browser-based agents. Server-side agents, MCP clients, and the CLI never send preflights and gain nothing from it.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/production.ts#cors -->
```ts
// Off unless set. Only browser-based agents need it.
cors: { origins: ["https://agent.example"], allowCredentials: true },
```
<!-- /include -->

With `cors` set, a preflight on any AXE path returns `204` with:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://agent.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization, AXE-Protocol
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
Vary: Origin
````

Every other response to a listed origin carries the same allow-origin header and exposes `AXE-Protocol`, `Retry-After`, and `RateLimit-Policy` so a browser client can read them. An origin not in the list gets a response with no CORS headers. With the wildcard as the origins value, credentials are never allowed, per the Fetch standard; set the credentials flag only when browser agents send cookies or `Authorization` headers to a listed origin.

## Caching the manifest

The manifest and each action definition are served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`. Change the number with the manifest cache option. The manifest changes only when you deploy, and the max-age is how long an agent that read it just before a deploy keeps calling an action you renamed.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/production.ts#cache -->
```ts
// Cache-Control: public, max-age=<seconds> on the manifest and on action definitions. Default 300.
manifestCacheSeconds: 600,
updatedAt: process.env.AXE_MANIFEST_UPDATED_AT ?? "2026-09-23T00:00:00Z",
```
<!-- /include -->

The manifest is public and identical for every anonymous request, so let your CDN cache it. Action invocations, `/axe/continue`, `/axe/resume`, and `/axe/poll` responses are per request and carry no cache header; do not add one at the CDN. On platforms the manifest varies by host, so the CDN key must include the host.

Set `updatedAt` from your build, for example from the commit timestamp. Agents and indexes use it to decide whether to re-read the manifest.

## Rate limiting

Declare your limit in `policies.rateLimit`. The SDK then emits `RateLimit-Policy` on every response, in the form `60;w=60`, so agents can pace themselves, and `Retry-After` on every `429`.

The SDK does not enforce the limit: it has no view of your fleet and would need yet another shared store for counters. Enforce at your edge, where you already rate limit the human site, or in `onRequest`, which runs before the handler on every action invocation and may short-circuit it with a result. Returning `fail` with `rate_limited` and the wait in `details` produces the `429` and the header:

<!-- include: examples/deploying/rate-limit.ts#hook -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Sunrise Yoga Studio",
  description:
    "Search upcoming yoga classes by date and style, see instructor names and spots left, and (once signed in) book or cancel a spot.",
  baseUrl: "https://sunriseyoga.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none"] },
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
  // Declared: the SDK emits RateLimit-Policy: 60;w=60 on every response.
  policies: { rateLimit: LIMIT },
  // Enforced: the SDK does not count requests. This hook does, and short-circuits the handler.
  onRequest: (ctx) => {
    const wait = take(callerKey(ctx));
    if (wait === 0) return;
    return fail("rate_limited", `Rate limit exceeded. Retry in ${wait} seconds.`, {
      retryable: true,
      // details.retryAfter becomes the Retry-After header on the 429.
      details: { retryAfter: wait },
    });
  },
});
```
<!-- /include -->

The bucket behind it:

<!-- include: examples/deploying/rate-limit.ts#bucket -->
```ts
// A token bucket per caller, in one process. Behind more than one instance, keep the
// buckets in Redis or enforce the limit at your edge instead.
const LIMIT = { requestsPerMinute: 60, burst: 20 };
const buckets = new Map<string, { tokens: number; updatedAt: number }>();

// Bearer token when the agent authenticates, otherwise the declared vendor.
function callerKey(ctx: HookContext): string {
  const bearer = ctx.request.headers.get("authorization");
  if (bearer) return `token:${bearer}`;
  return `vendor:${ctx.context.agent?.vendor?.toLowerCase() ?? "unknown"}`;
}

/** Returns 0 when the call is allowed, otherwise the number of seconds to wait. */
function take(key: string): number {
  const now = Date.now();
  const capacity = LIMIT.requestsPerMinute + LIMIT.burst;
  const perMs = LIMIT.requestsPerMinute / 60_000;
  const bucket = buckets.get(key) ?? { tokens: capacity, updatedAt: now };
  bucket.tokens = Math.min(capacity, bucket.tokens + (now - bucket.updatedAt) * perMs);
  bucket.updatedAt = now;
  buckets.set(key, bucket);
  if (bucket.tokens >= 1) {
    bucket.tokens -= 1;
    return 0;
  }
  return Math.max(1, Math.ceil((1 - bucket.tokens) / perMs / 1000));
}
```
<!-- /include -->

Key on the bearer token when there is one, because that is the identity you issued, and on the declared vendor otherwise; the vendor is self-reported, so it is a fairness key, not a security boundary. `onRequest` is not called for continuation, resume, or poll requests, which are gated by single-use tokens; limit those at the edge if you need to. Agents must honor `Retry-After` and must not retry a `rate_limited` error sooner; `@axe/client` does this for you.

## Observability hooks

Four hooks give you the request path. Each receives a `HookContext` with the endpoint (`action`, `continue`, `resume`, or `poll`), the action name (recovered from the token on the last three), the underlying `Request`, the sanitized request `context`, and the tenant on platforms.

| Hook        | Receives                           | When                                                                             | May return                        |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `onRequest` | the hook context                   | Before the handler on an action invocation, after auth and input validation.     | A result intent to short-circuit. |
| `onResult`  | the hook context, the `Result`     | After every result envelope is determined, on every endpoint, before it is sent. | Nothing.                          |
| `onError`   | the hook context, the thrown value | When a handler throws. The agent receives an `internal` error.                   | Nothing.                          |
| `onEvent`   | the `AXEEvent`                     | After the response is determined, asynchronously. See [Analytics](analytics.md). | Nothing.                          |

Wire `onRequest` and `onResult` to your structured logger with your own request id, `onError` to your APM client, and `onEvent` to a sink. The first three are request-scoped detail for your logs; the fourth is aggregate telemetry that is safe to ship anywhere.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/hooks.ts#fields -->
```ts
// The same fields on every line, so one request id ties the request, the result, and your
// own application logs together. The request id never enters an AXE event.
function fields(ctx: HookContext): Record<string, unknown> {
  return {
    requestId: ctx.request.headers.get("x-request-id"),
    endpoint: ctx.endpoint,
    action: ctx.action,
    vendor: ctx.context.agent?.vendor ?? "unknown",
    tenant: ctx.tenant?.id ?? null,
  };
}
```
<!-- /include -->

<!-- include: examples/deploying/hooks.ts#hooks -->
```ts
export const axe = createAXE({
  name: "Northgate University Admissions",
  description:
    "Check application status, upload transcripts and recommendation letters, and schedule campus visits for prospective students.",
  baseUrl: "https://admissions.northgate.example",
  auth: { modes: ["none", "user"], userLoginUrl: "https://admissions.northgate.example/login" },
  secret: process.env.AXE_SECRET,
  onRequest: (ctx) => {
    log.info({ msg: "axe.request", ...fields(ctx) });
  },
  onResult: (ctx, result) => {
    // Log the status, never result.output, result.accepts, or result.handoff.
    log.info({ msg: "axe.result", ...fields(ctx), status: result.status });
  },
  onError: (ctx, error) => {
    log.error({
      msg: "axe.error",
      ...fields(ctx),
      error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
    });
    apm.captureException(error, { action: ctx.action, endpoint: ctx.endpoint });
  },
  onEvent: otelSink({ meter: metrics.getMeter("axe") }),
});
```
<!-- /include -->

> **Warning**
> Never log `input`, `output`, or a continuation `payload`. A payload of a `sensitive` kind is a payment authorization or an identity document. The SDK validates it, hands it to `onContinue`, and forgets it. The hooks give you the result envelope so you can log its status; log nothing else from it.

`onResult` and `onError` failures are logged to stderr and the response goes out unchanged. An `onRequest` hook that throws an `AXEError` short-circuits with that error; any other exception propagates to your framework's error handler, so catch inside the hook.

## Rolling out one action at a time

Agents read the manifest and act on it, so an action that appears in production is in production. Grow the manifest one action at a time behind a flag, verifying at each step.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/flags.ts#gate -->
```ts
const trackOrder = action("orders.track", {
  title: "Track an order",
  description:
    "Returns the shipping status and estimated delivery date for one order, given the order number and the email used at purchase. Does not change anything.",
  readOnly: true,
  risk: "none",
  input: z.object({
    orderNumber: z.string().describe("Order number from the confirmation email, e.g. BG-48213"),
    email: z.string().email().describe("Email address used at purchase"),
  }),
  output: OrderStatus,
  display: {
    kind: "status",
    item: {
      id: "/orderNumber",
      title: "/orderNumber",
      url: "/url",
      attributes: [
        { label: "Status", path: "/status", format: "text" },
        { label: "Estimated delivery", path: "/estimatedDelivery", format: "date" },
      ],
    },
  },
  examples: [
    {
      input: { orderNumber: "BG-48213", email: "sam@example.com" },
      output: {
        orderNumber: "BG-48213",
        status: "shipped",
        estimatedDelivery: "2026-10-02",
        url: "https://bramblegoods.example/orders/BG-48213",
      },
    },
  ],
  handler: async ({ input }) => orders.status(input.orderNumber, input.email),
});

const startReturn = action("returns.start", {
  title: "Start a return",
  description:
    "Opens a return for a delivered order and returns a prepaid shipping label URL. The return can be cancelled from the order page until the package is scanned.",
  risk: "low",
  reversible: true,
  input: z.object({
    orderNumber: z.string().describe("Order number of a delivered order"),
    email: z.string().email().describe("Email address used at purchase"),
    reason: z.enum(["wrong-size", "damaged", "not-as-described", "other"]),
  }),
  output: z.object({ returnId: z.string(), labelUrl: z.string() }),
  handler: async ({ input }) => orders.startReturn(input.orderNumber, input.email, input.reason),
});

// Always on: a read-only action is the safest first step.
axe.register(trackOrder);
// Behind a flag: flip it for one environment, run the conformance suite, then flip it everywhere.
if (flags.isEnabled("axe.returns.start")) axe.register(startReturn);
```
<!-- /include -->

The order that works:

1. **One read-only action** with `readOnly: true` and `risk: "none"`. It cannot hurt anyone, and it exercises discovery, auth, and your adapter.
2. **Add `display`** so agents can present and compare results. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md).
3. **One mutating action**, low risk and reversible, with an affordance from the read action to it. Run the conformance suite with `--auth` so the ladder checks execute.
4. **Requirements**, when the mutating action needs something the agent may hold: a payment kind, an address, a consent. Watch the `needs_input` to `continued` ratio in your events.
5. **Handoffs**, last, for the steps that genuinely need the human. Verify the landing page calls `completeHandoff` and that resume works end to end. See [Human handoff](human-handoff.md).

At each step, run `axe conformance` against the deployed URL and `axe audit --min-score 80` in CI. The conformance suite fails the build when a check regresses; the audit threshold fails it when a new action ships without examples, without `display`, or with a description the linter rejects. [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md) has the CI configuration.

When an action must go, do not delete it; an MCP client configured last week still calls the old name. Mark it `deprecated` with `since` and `replacedBy`, keep it serving, and remove it once the events show no traffic:

<!-- include: examples/deploying/flags.ts#deprecate -->
```ts
// Keep the old name serving. Agents that read the manifest will move to orders.track on their own.
const lookupOrder = action("orders.lookup", {
  ...trackOrder.spec,
  title: "Look up an order (deprecated)",
  deprecated: { since: "2026-09-01", replacedBy: "orders.track" },
});
axe.register(lookupOrder);
```
<!-- /include -->

The replacement must be a registered action; the SDK refuses a `replacedBy` that points nowhere. [Deprecating actions](designing-actions.md#deprecating-actions) covers the agent-facing side.

## HTTPS, proxies, and baseUrl

`baseUrl` must use HTTPS. `createAXE` throws otherwise, with one exception: `localhost`, its subdomains, and the loopback addresses may use HTTP. Tokens travel in request bodies and keys in `Authorization` headers; neither has any protection but the transport.

A path prefix in `baseUrl` is honored. With a base of `https://www.oakridge-rentals.example/agents`, the manifest is at `/agents/.well-known/axe.json`, actions are under `/agents/axe/actions`, and the poll URLs and index links the SDK generates include the prefix. Serve the well-known path at the origin as well, as [Discovery](#discovery) says, because that is where agents look first.

<!-- include: examples/deploying/production.ts#baseurl -->
```ts
// HTTPS is required except for localhost. A path prefix is honored: every AXE path is served under it.
baseUrl: process.env.AXE_BASE_URL ?? "https://www.oakridge-rentals.example/agents",
```
<!-- /include -->

Behind a proxy or load balancer, the adapters rebuild the public URL of each request from the forwarded headers. The Express adapter reads the forwarded protocol and host and falls back to the socket; the Next.js Pages adapter reads the same headers and assumes HTTPS. If your proxy does not set them, pass `origin` to `axeExpress` or `axeNextPages` with your public origin so prefix routing and tenant resolution by host see what the agent sees. The fetch-based adapters (`axeFetch`, and `axeNext` for the App Router) receive a Web `Request` whose URL the framework already built; configure the framework's trusted-proxy setting instead. Terminate TLS at the proxy and keep the proxy-to-app hop on a private network.

## Checklist

Before the manifest is reachable from the public internet:

- [ ] `secret` is at least 16 characters and comes from a secret manager; no per-process-secret warning appears in the logs.
- [ ] `TokenStore` and `IdempotencyStore` are shared across instances, with TTLs honored.
- [ ] `baseUrl` is the public HTTPS origin agents will use, and `/.well-known/axe.json` answers there.
- [ ] `robots.txt` carries an `AXE-Manifest` line; `axe conformance` reports no hint warning.
- [ ] `policies.rateLimit` is declared, and the edge or `onRequest` enforces it.
- [ ] `cors` is unset unless browser-based agents are expected.
- [ ] `onError` reaches your APM; `onEvent` reaches a sink you will look at.
- [ ] No hook and no application log line contains `input`, `output`, or a continuation `payload`.
- [ ] The handoff landing page calls `completeHandoff`, and a resume works against the deployed URL.
- [ ] `axe conformance <url> --auth <token>` and `axe audit <url> --min-score 80` pass in CI.

## Next steps

- [Analytics](analytics.md): the event schema and the queries that tell you whether the rollout is working.
- [Security](security.md): the threat model, what the SDK mitigates, and what your site must.
- [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md): running the suites locally and in CI.
- [Platforms](platforms.md): serving many tenants, and the index.
````

# docs/api/README.md

# API reference

The pages under [`reference/`](reference/README.md) are generated by TypeDoc from the built packages: one page per package and one per entry point, listing every exported function, class, interface, and type with its signature, doc comment, and a link to the source line.

Do not edit anything under `reference/` by hand. Regenerate it from the repository root after changing a public signature or doc comment:

```sh
pnpm docs:api
```

The generator reads each package's source entry point through `typedoc.json` at the repository root and rewrites `docs/api/reference/` in full. This page is the only hand-written file in `docs/api/`.

## Packages

| Package | What it exports | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@axe/core` | The server runtime: `createAXE`, `action`, the result helpers (`needsInput`, `handoff`, `pending`, and the error helper), kinds and `accept`, token and idempotency stores, JSON Pointer utilities, the wire types. No framework dependencies. | [`@axe/core`](reference/@axe/core/README.md) |
| `@axe/client` | The agent side: `AXEClient` with `discover`, `invoke`, `continue`, `resume`, `poll`, and `run`, plus fulfillers and status type guards. No runtime dependencies. | [`@axe/client`](reference/@axe/client/README.md) |
| `@axe/mcp` | A Model Context Protocol server derived from an AXE server, manifest, or URL: `createMcpServer`, `serveStdio`, `serveHttp`. | [`@axe/mcp`](reference/@axe/mcp.md) |
| `@axe/express` | `axeExpress` for Express 4 and 5 and Connect-style frameworks, plus Node-to-Web request and response converters other Node adapters reuse. | [`@axe/express`](reference/@axe/express.md) |
| `@axe/next` | `axeNext` for App Router route files, `axeNextPages` for the Pages API. | [`@axe/next`](reference/@axe/next.md) |
| `@axe/fetch` | `axeFetch` for Hono, Remix, Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Deno, and SvelteKit, plus a path predicate for routers. | [`@axe/fetch`](reference/@axe/fetch.md) |
| `@axe/testing` | `runConformance`, `runAudit` and its weights, `createTestClient` for in-process tests, `checkVocabularyDrift`, sample payloads for every well-known kind. | [`@axe/testing`](reference/@axe/testing.md) |
| `@axe/surface` | `createSurface` (a registry of live controls with `observe`, `act`, and one revision), `useSurface` for React, and `surfaceActions`, which serves any surface as AXE actions with refusals mapped onto the ladder. | [`@axe/surface`](reference/@axe/surface/index.md), [`react`](reference/@axe/surface/react.md), [`axe`](reference/@axe/surface/axe.md) |
| `@axe/generate` | `fromOpenAPI`, `fromFunctions`, and `fromTRPCRouter` yield action candidates from definitions an application already has; `generate` applies overrides and policy, runs the honesty lints, and returns actions with provenance and warnings; `registerGenerated` registers them. | [`@axe/generate`](reference/@axe/generate.md) |
| `axe` | The CLI: `axe init`, `axe validate`, `axe inspect`, `axe preview`, `axe conformance`, `axe audit`, `axe mcp`, `axe generate`. The reference covers its programmatic surface; the commands are in [Getting started](../getting-started.md). | [`axe`](reference/axe.md) |

## Entry points of `@axe/core`

The main entry point re-exports the runtime and the most-used pieces of each subpath. The subpaths exist so agent-side and tooling code can import types or constants without pulling in Zod.

- [`@axe/core/kinds`](reference/@axe/core/kinds.md) — `kinds`, the typed well-known kind definitions; `accept` to build a requirement from one; helpers for custom `x-` kinds.
- [`@axe/core/events`](reference/@axe/core/events.md) — the event type and the sinks: `consoleSink`, `jsonlFileSink`, `otelSink`.
- [`@axe/core/display`](reference/@axe/core/display.md) — `resolveDisplay`, which applies a `display` declaration to an output and returns a presented result.
- [`@axe/core/lint`](reference/@axe/core/lint.md) — `lintAgentText` and `lintManifest`, and the patterns they match.
- [`@axe/core/schemas`](reference/@axe/core/schemas.md) — Zod schemas for every wire object, for validating documents you did not generate.
- [`@axe/core/vocabulary`](reference/@axe/core/vocabulary.md) — the `WIRE` constant: every path, header, status, error code, kind, field, and CLI name as a typed string.
- [`@axe/core/types`](reference/@axe/core/types.md) — the wire-level TypeScript types, with no runtime code.

## Where to start

**Integrating a site.** Read `createAXE` and `action` in the [`@axe/core` index](reference/@axe/core/index.md); together they are most of the API. Then `kinds` and `accept` in [`@axe/core/kinds`](reference/@axe/core/kinds.md) for requirements, and `needsInput` and `handoff` for the escalation ladder. Your framework's adapter is one function with one options object.

**Building an agent.** Start with `AXEClient` in the [`@axe/client` index](reference/@axe/client/index.md): `discover` finds a manifest from any URL, `run` drives the whole ladder with fulfillers and confirmation. Then [`@axe/client/present`](reference/@axe/client/present.md): `present` applies a `display` to a result, and `toMarkdown` or `toHTML` renders it.

## The vocabulary is generated

`WIRE` in `@axe/core/vocabulary` is generated from [`spec/VOCABULARY.md`](../../spec/VOCABULARY.md), not written by hand. A test regenerates it and fails if the committed file differs; the drift test fails if a wire name in the docs is missing from the vocabulary. To add or rename a wire name, edit the spec table and regenerate.

## Next steps

- [Getting started](../getting-started.md) to see the core API in use before reading signatures.
- [Concepts](../concepts.md) for what each exported piece is for.
- [For agent builders](../for-agent-builders.md) for the client and presentation packages end to end.
- [Glossary](../glossary.md) for the terms the reference assumes.

# docs/faq.md

# FAQ

Direct answers to the questions integrators and agent builders ask first. Where another standard does a job better, this page says so and shows how AXE defers to it or sits beside it.

### How is this different from MCP?

They solve different problems and compose. AXE is a site's declaration and HTTP protocol: a manifest at `/.well-known/axe.json`, actions invoked with plain JSON, a result envelope with an escalation ladder, and presentation hints. The Model Context Protocol is a transport and tool protocol between a model host and a server; it says how tools are listed and called, not what a business exposes or how it is found.

`@axe/mcp` derives an MCP server from any manifest: each action becomes a tool with the same JSON Schema, `needs_input` results list the accepted kinds and point at `axe_continue`, `needs_human` results carry the handoff text and point at `axe_resume`, and `pending` points at `axe_poll`. `axe mcp <url>` runs it over stdio; `serveHttp` mounts it on the Streamable HTTP transport.

What MCP alone does not give a site: discovery at a domain (there is no well-known path for "the MCP server for this business"), an escalation ladder (a tool either returns or errors), `display` hints, and human handoff semantics (no `resumeToken`, no `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`). If your only consumer is one MCP client, write the tool directly. If you want every agent to find you, write the manifest and derive the tools. Details in [MCP](mcp.md).

### How is this different from OpenAPI?

OpenAPI describes HTTP endpoints for developers: paths, verbs, parameters, response codes. AXE describes capabilities for agents: what an action does in a model-readable `description`, what it commits the user to (`risk`, `reversible`, `idempotent`), what it needs to finish (`accepts` with typed kinds), how to present its output (`display`), and what to do when a human must act (`handoff`).

You can generate an OpenAPI document from a manifest trivially: one `POST /axe/actions/{name}` operation per action, with the action's `input` and `output` schemas as the request and response bodies. The reverse loses the parts that matter: an OpenAPI document has no place for risk metadata, presentation, requirements a wallet can fulfill, or a resume token, and its `description` fields were written for a human reading a reference page. Keep OpenAPI for developers; AXE is a second, smaller surface for agents. The OpenAPI document is still a good place to start from: [`@axe/generate`](generating.md) derives the parts that carry over (names, flags, schemas, the HTTP call) and asks you for the rest instead of guessing.

### How is this different from llms.txt?

`llms.txt` is prose for a model to read: what a site is, where the important pages are, in Markdown. AXE is typed actions for a model to call. They complement each other and you should publish both if you have both: link the manifest from `llms.txt`, and put `humanFallbackUrl` and `contact` in the manifest so an agent that starts from either finds the other. A site with nothing to do beyond reading should stop at `llms.txt`; see [when not to use AXE yet](why-axe.md#when-you-should-not-use-axe-yet).

### How is this different from schema.org and JSON-LD?

schema.org describes things on pages: an event, an organization, an offer, marked up so a crawler can extract them. AXE describes actions: search, book, upload, apply, return. The well-known kind registry in [`spec/KINDS.md`](../spec/KINDS.md) is the analogue of schema.org vocabulary for requirement payloads: `contact.address`, `identity.government-id`, and `payment.ach-debit` are shared shapes so an agent's wallet and a site agree without negotiation. A site can carry both: keep JSON-LD on the pages for crawlers, and point `display.item.url` at those pages so agent-facing and human-facing data are the same thing.

### How is this different from Agent Protocol and A2A?

Agent Protocol and Agent2Agent are agent-to-agent: one agent delegates a task to another, with task lifecycles, artifacts, and messaging. AXE is site-to-agent: a business declares what it does and an agent calls it directly. An A2A agent that represents a business can wrap that business's AXE manifest, and an orchestrating agent can reach several AXE sites in one task. AXE assumes only that the caller can make HTTP requests and read JSON.

### Is this just SEO for agents?

In shape, yes, and the shape is deliberate. A discoverable declaration, agent-read descriptions, a shared vocabulary, presentation hints, an audit score, a conformance report, and opt-in directives: the [Why AXE](why-axe.md#the-seo-analogy-once) table maps each to its 2000s counterpart.

What the shape implies is a second thing the design takes seriously: SEO produced keyword stuffing, cloaking, and link farms, because a number could be moved by lying. So the protocol has [honesty rules](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#18-agent-facing-honesty): no instructions to the agent in any agent-read text, no superlatives, parity with the human page, at most six affordances per item, no custom kinds that duplicate well-known ones, consent scoped to what the action needs, truthful metadata. `axe audit` enforces what can be enforced and zeroes the Trustworthy category on an agent-directed imperative. The rest is the agents' job, as the next two answers explain.

### Will agents actually use it?

Adoption is the open question, and nobody can promise it. What makes it likely: discovery is one `GET` to a fixed path, so an agent framework can add AXE support in an afternoon; every manifest is an MCP server without extra work, so the agents people already run can use it today; and a structured `needs_input` or `needs_human` is strictly better for an agent than a screenshot of a form it could not complete.

What v0 does not solve: there is no directory or crawler, so an agent finds a site by starting from its URL, and there is no signed manifest or agent identity attestation. Platforms can publish an index at `/.well-known/axe-index.json` so their tenants are enumerable, and `robots.txt` can carry `AXE-Manifest` and `AXE-Index` lines for crawlers that look. The rest is in [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md).

### What stops a site from lying to agents?

Four things, in decreasing order of certainty.

1. **Registration and linting.** The SDK refuses a mutating action declared `readOnly`, an example that fails its own schema, a `display` pointer that resolves to nothing, and agent-read text that instructs the agent. `axe validate` runs the same checks in CI.
2. **Audit detection.** `axe audit` flags persuasion, affordance spam, structurally identical custom kinds, and consent bundles, and treats agent-directed imperatives and false `readOnly` as hard failures.
3. **Parity spot-check.** The audit prints the values an agent received next to `display.item.url` and, with a browser, looks for them on the human page. Cloaking is surfaced, not scored, because a false accusation on a dynamic page would teach teams to ignore the section.
4. **Reputation, which belongs to the agent.** There is no central authority. [Spec §18.3](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#183-reputation) says it plainly: agents build trust from observed parity, handoff rate, error rate, and whether `examples` match live responses, the way search engines built ranking from observed quality. A site that lies is ranked against by the agents it lies to.

### Do I need to rewrite my backend?

No. An action's `handler` is a function; it calls whatever your booking, admissions, leasing, or order code already does. Nothing in AXE requires a new database, a session store, or a state machine; the one interface you may implement is the [idempotency store](concepts.md#idempotency) for multi-instance deployments. Disclosure is progressive: start with one read-only action, as [Getting started](getting-started.md) does, and add a mutating action, a requirement, or a handoff when you are ready. Nothing shipped earlier changes.

### Does AXE process payments?

No, and it never holds card numbers. Payment kinds carry a credential your payment service provider can charge: `payment.card` is a PSP-issued token, `payment.ach-debit` is an authorization with the NACHA-required text, `payment.wire-confirmation` is a reference number after the fact, `payment.invoice` is billing details for net terms. Your `onContinue` hands the payload to the PSP you already use. The SDK validates the shape and never logs the payload. Payment execution and tokenization are out of scope by design; see [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md).

### What about authentication and OAuth?

Three modes: `none` for public reads, `site` for an API key you issue to an agent operator (your `verifySiteKey` function decides), and `user` for acting on behalf of a specific person. In `user` mode an agent can pass through a bearer token the person already granted it, mapped to `onBehalfOf` by your `authenticate` function; when no identity can be established, the server returns a `login_required` handoff to your `userLoginUrl`, and the resume token is bound to whoever signs in. The claimed identity in the request body is never trusted.

No OAuth 2.1 authorization server ships in v0. Most sites have one or use a vendor, and running one is its own product. [Auth](auth.md) shows where yours plugs in: its access tokens go through `authenticate`, its authorization endpoint becomes `userLoginUrl`.

### Can I use it from Python or Go?

The wire protocol is plain JSON over HTTPS with published JSON Schemas for the manifest, the request, the result envelope, the index, the event, and every kind, under [`spec/schemas/`](../spec/schemas/). A server in another language serves a manifest, validates input against JSON Schema, signs HMAC-SHA256 tokens, and returns envelopes. An agent client is a `GET` and a `POST`. Nothing depends on TypeScript or Zod. SDKs for other languages are deferred until the protocol settles; see [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md). `axe conformance` runs against any URL, so a port proves itself the same way the reference does.

### How do I opt a specific agent out?

Declare it in `policies.agents`. `deny` wins over `allow`; an absent `allow` permits every vendor not denied. Matching is exact and case-insensitive against `context.agent.vendor`.

```json
{
  "policies": {
    "agents": { "deny": ["ScrapeCo"] }
  }
}
```

Agents must not call actions on a site whose policy denies their vendor; servers built with the SDK also enforce it and return `forbidden`. The directives in `robots.txt` are discovery hints only and say nothing about access; the policy is the mechanism. See [spec §3.4](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#34-opting-out).

## Next steps

- [Why AXE](why-axe.md): the problem, the analogy, and when to wait.
- [MCP](mcp.md): the derived server and its limits.
- [Auth](auth.md): the three modes and the v1 OAuth path.
- [Security](security.md): the threat model and what your site must still do.

# docs/glossary.md

# Glossary

Every term in these docs, alphabetically, linking to the page that defines it. Code-font names are spelled as [`spec/VOCABULARY.md`](../spec/VOCABULARY.md) spells them.

**action** — One thing an agent can do on a site: a namespaced name such as `classes.search`, agent-facing `title` and `description`, `input` and `output` schemas, safety metadata (`readOnly`, `idempotent`, `reversible`, `risk`, `auth`), and a handler. See [Concepts](concepts.md#action).

**affordance** — A follow-up action that makes sense for an item in a result, with inputs pre-bound. A _static_ affordance is declared under `affordances` with JSON Pointer bindings. A _dynamic_ affordance is returned at runtime under `_axe` with concrete inputs. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md#affordances).

**agent** — Software acting for a user by reading a manifest and calling actions: a chat assistant with tools, an MCP client, a batch process. Agents identify themselves in `context.agent` and the `User-Agent` header. See [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md).

**agent-read text** — Every string a model reads from a manifest or result: descriptions, titles, `message`, `instructions`, `disclaimer`, labels, badges, error messages. Subject to the honesty rules and linted at registration. See [spec §18.1](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#181-agent-read-text).

**audit** — `axe audit`, or `runAudit` behind it. Fetches a live site, scores it across five categories (Discoverable, Describable, Presentable, Actionable, Trustworthy), and prints a fix list ordered by impact. See [Audit](audit.md).

**availability** — The optional `availability` an action declares: `{ available: true }` or `{ available: false, reason, requires?, handoff? }`, computed for the caller when the manifest or `/axe/state` is rendered. A report, not a gate: the handler still refuses, with `unavailable`. See [Live state and revisions](live-state.md#availability-unavailable-because).

**AXE Score** — The 0 to 100 number an audit produces. One hard failure, agent-directed text, zeroes it regardless of the rest. See [Audit](audit.md).

**brand hints** — The optional `brand` object on a manifest: `name`, `logoUrl`, `accentColor`, `tone`. Renderers may use them and must treat them as hints. See [spec §13.2](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#132-brand-hints).

**conformance** — Whether a live server satisfies every numbered requirement of the spec. `axe conformance` runs the suite against a URL and reports pass, fail, warn, or skip per check. See [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md#reading-the-report).

**continuation token** — The signed, opaque `continuationToken` in a `needs_input` result, sent back to `/axe/continue` with a `kind` and `payload`. Single-use, valid about 15 minutes. See [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md).

**display** — The optional `display` object on an action: where the list is, the item's `id`, `title`, `url`, `price`, `attributes`, and the `disclaimer` that must accompany any rendering. Data about data, never markup. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md#annotating-an-output-schema).

**drift test** — The `@axe/testing` check (`checkVocabularyDrift`) that scans every Markdown page for inline code spans that look like wire names and fails when one is not in the vocabulary. See [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md).

**escalation ladder** — The order a site responds in when an action cannot complete: `ok`; otherwise ask the agent for something it may hold (`needs_input`); otherwise hand off to the human (`needs_human`). See [Concepts](concepts.md#the-escalation-ladder).

**event** — The one record emitted per handled request: action, `status`, `ladder`, vendor, `latencyMs`, `kind`, `errorCode`, `tenant`. No payloads, no identities. Delivered to the sinks passed to `onEvent`. See [Analytics](analytics.md).

**flow** — A named path through the affordance graph, declared under `flows` with action names as `steps`. Carries no state and imposes no order. See [Concepts](concepts.md#flows).

**fulfiller** — On the agent side, an object that produces a payload for one or more kinds: a wallet, a credential store. `AXEClient` consults its `fulfillers` on `needs_input`. See [For agent builders](for-agent-builders.md).

**handoff** — A structured request that a human do one thing on the site: `reason`, `instructions`, a `url` landing on the step, a `resumeToken`, `expiresAt`, and `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`. Returned as `needs_human` or attached to `needs_input` as `fallback`. See [Human handoff](human-handoff.md).

**honesty rules** — The seven rules in spec §18 for agent-read text and metadata: no instructions to the agent, no persuasion, parity with the human site, affordance restraint, no fake kinds, scoped consent, truthful metadata. See [Audit](audit.md#honesty-rules).

**idempotency key** — The `idempotencyKey` sent with every mutating call. Replaying it with the same input returns the original result without re-running the handler; with different input, `conflict`. See [Concepts](concepts.md#idempotency).

**index** — Also _platform index_. The paginated list of tenant manifests a platform serves at `/.well-known/axe-index.json`: `platform`, `sites` with a `manifestUrl` each, `next` for the following page. Tenant manifests point back with `indexUrl`. See [Platforms](platforms.md#publish-axe-indexjson).

**kind** — The namespaced name of what a requirement asks for. _Well-known_ kinds come from [`spec/KINDS.md`](../spec/KINDS.md), so an agent's wallet can fulfill them automatically. _Custom_ kinds are yours, named `x-<org>.<name>`. See [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md).

**live state** — The optional `live` member of a manifest and the document at `/axe/state`: the site's current `rev` and every action's `availability`, served uncached and per caller. See [Live state and revisions](live-state.md).

**manifest** — The JSON document at `/.well-known/axe.json` an agent reads first: `name`, `description`, `baseUrl`, `auth`, every action, `policies`, `contact`, `brand`. Generated by `describe`, never written by hand. See [Concepts](concepts.md#manifest).

**`needs_human`** — The result status meaning only a human can do the next step. Carries a `handoff`. See [Human handoff](human-handoff.md).

**`needs_input`** — The result status meaning the agent may be able to supply what is missing. Carries `reason`, `message`, an ordered `accepts` list, a `continuationToken`, and an optional `fallback`. See [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md).

**`pending`** — The result status for work that outlasts a request. Carries `pollUrl` and `retryAfter`; the agent polls until a terminal result appears. Produced with `pending`, completed by `onPoll`. See [Concepts](concepts.md#the-result-envelope).

**pointer** — An RFC 6901 JSON Pointer such as `/units` or `/price/amount`. Every `display` location and static affordance binding is one. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md).

**presented result** — An `ok` result with its `display` applied: items with resolved title, URL, price, attributes, badges, and affordances, ready for `toMarkdown` or `toHTML`. Produced by `present` in `@axe/client/present`. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md).

**primary affordance** — The one affordance per item marked `primary`: the default next step. At most one per item. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md#affordances).

**protocol version** — `axe/0.1`, carried in the manifest `protocol` field, the index, and the `AXE-Protocol` header. Minor versions are compatible; a different major is `unsupported`. See [spec §2](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#2-versioning).

**requirement** — One entry in `accepts`: a `kind`, `title`, `description`, JSON `schema`, whether it is `sensitive`, and optional `instructions` the agent relays. Built with `accept`. See [Requirements and kinds](requirements-and-kinds.md).

**reserved key `_axe`** — The one member name a site may not use for its own data in an output or item. It carries protocol extensions, today dynamic affordances, and is stripped before display resolution. See [Presenting results](presenting-results.md#affordances).

**result envelope** — The single JSON object every response is: a `status` of `ok`, `needs_input`, `needs_human`, `pending`, or `error`, plus that status's members. Agents branch on `status`, never on the HTTP code. See [Concepts](concepts.md#the-result-envelope).

**resume token** — The signed, opaque `resumeToken` in a handoff. After the human acts, the agent posts it to `/axe/resume` and `onResume` runs with the original state. Single-use, valid about 24 hours. See [Human handoff](human-handoff.md).

**revision** — One opaque value (`rev`) for the whole site that moves with every change an agent could observe, whoever made it. Returned on every result envelope; presented by the agent as `expectedRev`; a mismatch is `conflict` with `expectedRev` and `currentRev` in `details`, and nothing applied. See [Live state and revisions](live-state.md#the-revision).

**risk** — The declared consequence level of an action: `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`. Agents decide how much to confirm from it; declaring it truthfully is an honesty rule. See [Designing actions](designing-actions.md#choosing-risk).

**sensitive** — The `sensitive` flag on a requirement: the payload is a credential, payment instrument, or personal data. Agents confirm before sending it; it is never logged or put in events. See [Security](security.md).

**site** — In prose, the organization exposing an AXE surface. As the `site` auth mode, the agent itself authenticates with an API key in `Authorization`, checked by `verifySiteKey`. See [Auth](auth.md).

**state** — The JSON value a handler attaches to `needsInput`, `handoff`, or `pending`. It never crosses the wire: stored server-side under the token id and delivered to `onContinue`, `onResume`, or `onPoll`. See [Concepts](concepts.md#handoff-and-resume).

**tenant** — One site among many on a platform: a `TenantInfo` with a stable `id`, its own `baseUrl`, and overrides for the manifest fields that differ between sites. Resolved per request, passed to every handler, recorded on every event as `tenant`. See [Platforms](platforms.md).

**vendor** — The organization operating an agent, sent as `context.agent.vendor`. What `policies.agents` matches for `allow` and `deny`, and what events record. See [spec §17](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md#17-agent-identification-and-rate-limits).

**`whatAgentShouldSayToUser`** — The handoff field that tells the agent how to frame the human step in its own voice: what is needed, why, and that it will continue afterward. Agent-read text, never instructions to the agent. See [Human handoff](human-handoff.md).

## Next steps

- [Concepts](concepts.md) puts these terms together in order.
- [`spec/VOCABULARY.md`](../spec/VOCABULARY.md) is the exact spelling of every name.
- [Protocol spec](../spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md) is the normative definition behind each entry.

# docs/site.md

# The website

The marketing and documentation site lives in `site/` and is built into `site/dist/`, which is committed. Opening `site/dist/index.html` from disk renders the landing page and every documentation page with no server and no network: the site is plain HTML, one stylesheet, and one classic script, and it deploys as static files anywhere that can serve a directory.

## How it is built

`pnpm site:build` runs `site/build.mjs` (the site is deliberately outside `pnpm -r build`, because rendering the Open Graph image needs a browser), which:

1. Renders every Markdown page in `docs/`, `spec/`, and the repository root (README, roadmap, decisions, changelog, contributing, security) into `site/dist/docs/` with the documentation template: a sidebar generated from the ordered list in `docs/README.md`, an "On this page" rail from the headings, previous and next links in that same order, and an "Edit this page" link.
2. Rewrites relative Markdown links to the generated pages and fails the build on any link that does not resolve to a page, an existing anchor, or a file in the output.
3. Highlights code with Shiki at build time, emitting light and dark colors as CSS variables so no highlighter ships to the browser, and adds a copy button to every block.
4. Renders Mermaid diagrams to inline SVG at build time with a pure-JavaScript renderer, with a text version of each diagram behind a disclosure.
5. Fills the landing page's include markers from the docs' own sources: code blocks come from `docs/examples/`, prose excerpts come from `docs/why-axe.md`, the docs hub comes from `docs/README.md`, and the demo data comes from running `docs/examples/apartments/site.ts` in-process with the clock and random ids pinned, so the envelopes are real and the build is reproducible.
6. Embeds a search index as JSON in each page and generates `sitemap.txt` and the Open Graph image.

Nothing on the site is a hand-copied version of something in the repository. If a sentence on the landing page needs to change, change the doc it is pulled from.

## Adding a documentation page

You do not touch the site. Add the page to `docs/`, link it from the ordered list in `docs/README.md`, and rebuild: the sidebar, the previous and next links, the search index, and the docs hub all derive from that list. To place the page on the landing page's hub, add its path to the group map at the top of `site/build.mjs`.

## Running the tests

`pnpm site:test` runs `site/test/run.mjs`:

- **reproducible**: two builds are byte-identical, and the committed `site/dist/` matches a fresh build.
- **offline**: every page loads from `file://` in Chromium with all network requests aborted, with zero console errors, failed requests, or broken images; the landing page and one docs page also load in Firefox and WebKit.
- **links**: every `href` and `src` in the output resolves; external links point only at the repository and npm.
- **demos**: the ladder demo plays both paths and reports the expected `status` sequence; choosing a unit in the rendered search binds its id into the ladder; search and the theme toggle work from the keyboard.
- **screenshots**: the landing page at four widths in light and dark, compared with the baselines committed under `site/test/__screenshots__/`. Regenerate them with `node site/test/run.mjs --update-screenshots` and look at them.
- **llms**: `llms.txt` starts with a title and summary, every link in it resolves in the repository and in the published copy, and `llms-full.txt` carries every docs and spec page.
- **lighthouse**: performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO at 95 or above on the landing page and one docs page, served over a local port for the run.

CI builds the site and fails if `site/dist/` differs from the committed output. The Open Graph image is rendered by a browser and excluded from that byte comparison.

## Iterating

`pnpm site:dev` serves `site/dist/` on a local port for convenience while editing. The deliverable never needs it.

## Next steps

- [Testing and conformance](testing-and-conformance.md) for the checks the site's demos are built on.
- [Contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md) for the repository layout.
- [Docs index](README.md).

# spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md

# AXE Protocol Specification

**Version:** `axe/0.1`
**Status:** Draft. The protocol may change before 1.0. Changes are recorded in `CHANGELOG.md` and reasoned about in `DECISIONS.md`.
